title: Apple HomeView: Everything you need to know about Apple’s smart-home display
content:
Macworld





Apple HomeView is Apple’s first dedicated smart-home display, combining a 7-inch touchscreen, powerful speakers, a camera, and Siri AI in a device designed to sit at the center of the connected home. Announced on October 13, 2026, it brings together smart-home controls, entertainment, video calling, calendars, reminders, and other everyday information.
Powered by Apple’s A18 chip and Apple Intelligence, HomeView offers a much more capable version of Siri that can answer questions conversationally, help with everyday tasks, and access personal information from a compatible iPhone or iPad. It can also recognize up to six members of a household, providing a personalized experience while keeping individual information private.
HomeView is designed to work alongside Apple’s existing HomePod speakers, Apple TV, iPhone, and iPad. It integrates with the Apple Home app, supporting compatible HomeKit and Matter accessories, including lights, locks, thermostats, and security cameras. It can also serve as a central smart-home hub, making it easier to manage devices and automations throughout the house.
Unlike a HomePod with a screen added, HomeView is designed around visual interaction as well as voice control. Its touchscreen, customizable widgets, FaceTime camera, personalized Home Screens, and dedicated smart-home dashboards make it more like a shared household computer than a conventional smart speaker. It comes in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, with prices starting at $299/£299.
What can Apple HomeView do?
HomeView introduces a range of capabilities that aren’t available on Apple’s traditional HomePod speakers. While HomePod focuses primarily on music, Siri, and voice-controlled smart-home functions, HomeView adds a touchscreen, camera, personalized interface, and much deeper integration with Apple apps and services.

Music and videoView album artwork, lyrics, videos, and supported streaming content on the built-in display
Photos and customizable facesDisplay shared albums, photo collections, clocks, weather, and animated faces
Messages and communicationRead and respond to messages, make calls, and use Intercom
Recipes and household activitiesFollow step-by-step cooking instructions, manage timers, and access helpful information

 



HomeView also supports Handoff from iPhone, Live Activities, Find My, and multiroom audio with compatible AirPlay speakers.
How does HomeView compare with HomePod and iPad?
The biggest difference between HomeView and HomePod is the display. While a HomePod can control smart-home devices and play music using Siri, HomeView provides an interactive dashboard and visual feedback, making it more useful for managing a busy household.
HomeView also offers capabilities that make it a potential alternative to an iPad in certain situations. It can display recipes, calendars, photos, and video calls without needing someone to pick it up or unlock it. Its ability to recognize different household members and switch automatically between personalized experiences is particularly useful in a shared space.
However, HomeView isn’t intended to replace an iPad. The iPad remains the better choice for portable computing, productivity, games, and the broad selection of apps available from the App Store. HomeView is designed to stay in one place and provide convenient access to household information, entertainment, and smart-home controls.


Apple HomeView release date: When will it go on sale?
Announced: October 13, 2026 
Pre-orders: October 13, 2026 
In Store: November 13, 2026
Apple announced HomeView on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of its “Welcome home” launch. Pre-orders opened the same day, with both the tabletop and wall-mounted models scheduled to go on sale on Friday, November 13.
HomeView is initially available in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India, New Zealand, Singapore, and South Africa. Singapore pre-orders open on October 15, while customers in South Africa can order through authorized resellers.
The device won’t initially be sold in the European Union because Siri AI isn’t currently available in iOS in the EU. Apple says it is working toward resolving the situation, but hasn’t announced a European release date.
HomeView can be ordered from the Apple website, Apple Store app, and selected retailers. It will also be displayed in Apple Stores. Apple hasn’t announced any general shipping delays beyond the roughly one-month gap between its announcement and retail availability, although individual delivery estimates may vary.
The November 13 date confirms the mid-November launch timeframe reported before the announcement. Earlier speculation about an October 30 launch is now superseded by Apple’s official schedule.
Pre-order HomeView from Apple U.S. 
Pre-order HomeView from Apple U.K. 


							


Apple HomeView design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			The HomeView

Apple




HomeView has a compact, square display mounted above a rounded aluminum speaker base, with a design that recalls Apple’s classic iMac G4. A stainless steel hinge allows the screen to tilt, making it easy to adjust the viewing angle when HomeView is positioned on a kitchen counter, desk, or bedside table.
The tabletop model is available in four colors: Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray. The base incorporates the speakers, including a downward-firing woofer, while the display contains two additional full-range drivers. Apple uses 100 percent recycled aluminum in the base and includes a color-matched USB-C power cable.
The wall-mounted HomeView has a different design, with a slim square enclosure that’s just 0.39 inch thick. It is available in Silver and Space Gray and is designed for locations such as hallways and entrances. Unlike the tabletop model, it doesn’t include a separate woofer and requires a compatible wall mount, sold separately.
Both versions feature a touchscreen, built-in camera, four microphones, and USB-C power. Apple hasn’t listed conventional volume or power buttons in the published specifications, with touch and Siri providing the primary controls.


						

							




HomeView dimensions and weight

ColorsSilver, Starlight, Rose Pink, Space GraySilver, Space Gray

 The tabletop dimensions vary depending on the display’s tilt angle.






Does Apple HomeView have a camera?
Yes. Both HomeView models feature a built-in 12-megapixel Center Stage camera with an f/2.4 aperture.
The camera supports FaceTime video calling, with Center Stage automatically adjusting the framing to keep people visible as they move around or when additional participants join the conversation. Four beamforming microphones help pick up voices from across the room while reducing background noise.
The camera also plays an important role in HomeView’s personalized features. It can recognize registered household members by face, automatically switching to their individual Home Screen and making their personal information available when the required security conditions are met.
Apple uses a protected processing environment called Secure Exclaves to isolate facial and voice recognition data from the operating system and apps. The system is designed so that the sensitive camera and microphone information used for recognition isn’t exposed to other users or Apple.
Apple hasn’t published more detailed video recording specifications, such as maximum capture resolution or frame rate.


						

							


What screen does Apple HomeView have?

				
					

				
			
HomeView

Foundry




HomeView features a 7-inch Liquid Retina touchscreen with a resolution of 1088 by 1088 pixels, giving it a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. It uses an LED-backlit IPS panel with Multi-Touch support, True Tone, and a fingerprint-resistant oleophobic coating.
Maximum brightness reaches 500 nits, while minimum brightness drops to just 0.3 nits, making it suitable for a bedside table without lighting up the room at night.
The interface also adapts to proximity, showing simpler information when viewed from across the room and revealing more detail as someone approaches. Customizable faces include Photos, Calendar, Weather, Flow, and Snoopy.
The display is the same on the tabletop and wall-mounted models. Apple hasn’t specified a refresh rate, and there’s no OLED option.


						

							


What processor does Apple HomeView use?
HomeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, the same generation of processor introduced with the iPhone 16 in 2024. This is considerably more powerful than the Apple Watch-derived processors used in older HomePod models and gives HomeView the processing capabilities needed for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.
The A18 is manufactured using a second-generation 3-nanometer process. In its original iPhone implementation, it features a six-core CPU, five-core GPU, and 16-core Neural Engine. Apple hasn’t confirmed whether the HomeView uses exactly the same CPU and GPU configuration, or whether the chip has been adapted for the new device.
The Neural Engine is particularly important because HomeView uses AI to support conversational Siri interactions, recognize household members, process camera and microphone information, and provide personalized responses. Apple’s Secure Exclaves also isolate sensitive recognition data from the operating system and applications.
Apple hasn’t revealed any performance comparisons between HomeView and previous HomePod processors, or disclosed any HomeView-specific improvements to chip packaging or manufacturing. However, the A18’s efficient 3nm architecture should help Apple deliver substantial processing power in a compact device that’s designed to operate continuously.
The A18 was one of the key specifications correctly predicted in our earlier HomeView rumors.


						

							




Apple HomeView connectivity and compatibility
HomeView supports Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread networking, giving it the wireless connectivity needed to communicate with Apple devices and compatible smart-home accessories.


ConnectivityHomeView specification

Wi-FiWi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO
Wi-Fi bandsSimultaneous dual-band operation
BluetoothBluetooth 6.0
ThreadSupported
MatterCompatible accessories supported
HomeKit / Apple HomeSupported

Ultra WidebandNot listed in Apple’s specifications
Cellular modemNo cellular connectivity announced
Satellite connectivityNot supported or advertised
Wired connectionUSB-C for power

 



HomeView integrates directly with Apple’s Home app and can control compatible smart lights, door locks, thermostats, blinds, and security cameras. It also supports Matter accessories, expanding compatibility beyond devices specifically designed for HomeKit.
Importantly, HomeView can act as a home hub itself. You don’t need to buy a separate HomePod or Apple TV simply to use HomeView as your smart-home hub. However, some advanced features depend on compatible accessories, an iCloud+ subscription, or an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. 
Apple has also announced the Apple Home Collection, a new lineup of cameras, thermostats, and a smart lock developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The first accessories will arrive in December 2026, with additional products following in early 2027.


Which iPhones and iPads work with HomeView?
Apple lists an iPhone running iOS 27.2 or later or an iPad running iPadOS 27.2 or later as a system requirement, alongside Wi-Fi internet access.
To use HomeView’s more personalized Siri AI features, you’ll need a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Basic Siri AI functions, including general questions and conversational interactions, remain available without an Apple Intelligence-enabled companion device.
HomeView also requires an Apple Account and compatible paired device for each household member who wants access to their personal information.


						

							


Does Apple HomeView have a battery or MagSafe charging?
Neither HomeView model has a built-in battery. Both are designed to remain connected to a power supply, so you can’t pick one up and use it around the house like an iPad.
The standard tabletop model includes a 1.5-meter USB-C cable and a 30W power adapter. Its USB-C connection supplies power rather than functioning as a conventional charging port.
The wall-mounted HomeView also requires continuous power, but Apple doesn’t include the wall mount, USB-C cable, or power adapter. These must be purchased separately, with a minimum 20W power adapter required when using a compatible USB-C power arrangement.
Apple offers three mounting solutions through Schneider Home, including a plug-in USB-C option, an AC-wired installation, and a Power over Ethernet (PoE) version coming in early 2027.


						

							


What software does Apple HomeView use?

				
					

				
			
Like a big Apple Watch

Apple




HomeView runs dedicated home-focused software built around Siri AI, Apple’s Home app, widgets, and a selection of familiar Apple applications. Apple identifies the initial Siri AI software as HomeView software version 27.2.
Rather than providing a conventional iPad interface, HomeView is designed to show useful information at a glance and respond to touch, voice, and proximity. Users can customize their Home Screen with apps and widgets, while special faces display photos, clocks, weather, calendar information, and animated artwork.
What can Siri AI do on HomeView?
Siri AI is one of HomeView’s biggest selling points. Powered by Apple Intelligence, it can answer open-ended questions, understand follow-up requests, draw on broad world knowledge, and support natural conversations.
For example, users can ask Siri to find a recipe, explain something they’re interested in, recommend music, control their smart-home accessories, or help organize everyday tasks.
When HomeView is paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri becomes more personal. It can draw on information from Calendar, Messages, and other apps, helping users locate an invitation, check an appointment, or find relevant information without manually searching their devices.
Siri conversations can also continue across Apple devices using the Siri app, with conversation history privately synced through iCloud.
There are some limitations. Siri AI initially supports English, with Canadian French coming later. Certain AI features that use server-side models have daily usage limits, and Apple says expanded access will eventually be available for a fee. Siri AI launches in beta on HomeView software 27.2.


						

							




Which apps are available on HomeView?
Apple includes a selection of built-in apps and provides access to additional entertainment services through compatible iPhones.


Built-in appsAdditional apps and content

Calendar, Reminders, MessagesApple TV
FaceTime, Find My, IntercomApple News
Music, PodcastsAudiobooks
Home, SafariApple Music Classical
Weather, World ClockCompatible third-party audio and video apps
Alarms, Timers, SettingsSupported content and services from iPhone

 



HomeView supports third-party audio and video apps from compatible iPhones, but Apple hasn’t announced a dedicated HomeView App Store or general installation of iPad apps. That means it shouldn’t be regarded as a replacement for an iPad’s broader software capabilities.


How does HomeView work for different family members?
HomeView can recognize up to six users by their faces, automatically switching between personalized Home Screens and keeping each person’s content separate.
For example, one family member could approach HomeView and see their own calendar and reminders, while another would be shown different information. Shared photo albums, music, and general smart-home controls can still be enjoyed by everyone.
Access to personal information is more tightly controlled. The user’s paired iPhone or iPad must be on the same Wi-Fi network, must have been recently unlocked, and HomeView must recognize the person’s face.
Guests and unrecognized users can still ask Siri questions, play music, check the weather, set timers, and control eligible smart-home accessories, without gaining access to anyone’s private messages or calendars.


						

							


Is Apple HomeView secure?
Apple has designed HomeView with a particular emphasis on privacy, given that it includes an always-available camera and microphones in a shared household space.
The A18 chip uses Secure Exclaves to process camera and microphone data used for recognizing faces and voices. This information is isolated from the operating system and apps, so sensitive recognition data isn’t exposed to other software or Apple.
For Siri requests, HomeView can process information locally or use Private Cloud Compute, which Apple says handles cloud requests without storing the data or making it accessible to Apple.
HomeView also supports HomeKit Secure Video, including intelligent recognition of people, pets, packages, and vehicles with a compatible iCloud+ subscription. It can provide AI-generated descriptions of recorded activity, although these advanced features require setup with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.


						

							


How much does Apple HomeView cost?
Apple HomeView $299/£299
Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) $299/£299
Apple HomeView starts at $299 in the U.S. and £299 in the U.K., with the tabletop and wall-mounted models carrying the same base price.
This positions HomeView below the $349 full-size HomePod price, although HomeView isn’t necessarily a direct replacement for that audio-focused speaker. 


						

							




Do HomeView wall mounts cost extra?
Yes. While the tabletop HomeView includes the accessories needed for power, the wall-mounted version requires additional purchases.


Schneider Home mounting accessoryU.S. priceAvailability

Power Mount USB-C Wall ConnectorFrom $59.95/£54.95Pre-order now
Power Mount AC WiredFrom $79.95/£69.95Pre-order now
Power Mount PoE Wired$129.95/£119.95Early 2027

 



For U.S. customers, this brings the minimum hardware cost of the wall-mounted HomeView and listed USB-C mount to $358.95, before any additional installation or power accessories.


Should you buy Apple HomeView?
Apple HomeView looks particularly appealing for households already invested in Apple’s ecosystem. It brings together smart-home controls, a capable Siri assistant, video calling, entertainment, and personalized information in a single device that can be shared by everyone at home.
For families, its biggest advantage could be convenience. Being able to see calendars, reminders, weather, timers, and security cameras in a central location, while automatically switching between household members, makes HomeView more useful than a conventional smart speaker.
It’s also attractive for people with extensive HomeKit or Matter smart-home setups. Rather than relying on an iPhone whenever they want to adjust the heating, check a security camera, or activate a scene, users get a dedicated interface that’s always available.
However, HomeView won’t be essential for everyone. If you mainly use Siri to play music, set timers, and control a handful of smart lights, a HomePod mini is a considerably cheaper option. And if you already use an iPad on a stand in the kitchen, you may find that it handles many of the same tasks while offering much greater flexibility.
At $299/£299, HomeView is a premium alternative to smart displays from Amazon and Google. Its strongest selling points are its integration with Apple products, privacy-focused recognition of individual users, and the more powerful Siri AI experience. However, it’s worth remembering that some of those personalized AI features require a recent Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.


						

							


Which HomeView model should you buy?
For most people, the standard tabletop HomeView is the more sensible choice. It costs the same as the wallmounted version but includes a more substantial speaker system, an adjustable display, and the power accessories needed to get started.
The wallmounted version makes more sense if you want a permanent smarthome control panel in a hallway, entrance, or other shared area. Its slim design is more discreet, although the additional cost of mounting accessories and potentially professional installation makes it less affordable.
We’d recommend waiting for independent reviews before deciding whether HomeView’s sound quality, Siri performance, and personalized features justify its price. But for Apple households looking for a central smart-home display, HomeView already offers a combination of features that no existing HomePod can match.

title: M6 MacBook Pro: Everything we know about Apple’s next laptop
content:
Macworld





Apple offers the MacBook Pro with three different chip options. It starts with the entry-level M5 chip, which you can only get in the 14-inch MacBook Pro. Apple also offers higher end M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro, as it has since the M1 arrived in 2020.
Apple launched the M5 MacBook Pro in October 2025, and the next generation could arrive almost exactly a year later. According to a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple plans to announce the entry-level 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro on October 27, alongside a new iMac, iPad mini, and the first touchscreen MacBook Pro.
The standard M6 MacBook Pro is expected to retain the existing design, with the new processor providing the main upgrade. The more substantial changes—including an OLED touchscreen and redesigned chassis—are reportedly reserved for premium MacBook Pro models that will continue to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. Apple is reportedly skipping the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation to accelerate development of the M7.
That creates an unusual buying decision: wait for the M6 chip, choose one of the redesigned touchscreen models, or hold out until 2027 for the next generation. Here’s what the latest reports suggest.s.


M6 MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
• October 27, 2026 (reported announcement date)
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on October 8 that Apple is planning to announce the M6 MacBook Pro on October 27, 2026. According to the report, the launch will include an online video presentation and an in-person component for the press.
The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to launch alongside the first OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro, an M6 iMac, and an updated iPad mini. The new entry-level MacBook Pro is expected to retain its 14-inch display and existing design, with the M6 chip providing the main upgrade.
The reported October 27 announcement would fit Apple’s recent release pattern. The M5 MacBook Pro arrived in October 2025, while its predecessor launched in November 2024.
Of the five generations of the entry-level MacBook Pro, three have been released in the October/November timeframe, including the past two releases. Here are the release dates for the entry-level MacBook Pro:
M5 MacBook Pro: October 2025
M4 MacBook Pro: November 2024
M3 MacBook Pro: January 2023
M2 MacBook Pro: June 2022
M1 MacBook Pro: November 2020
Ongoing memory and storage chip shortages could still affect availability or delivery times. These supply constraints have already contributed to price increases across Apple’s Mac lineup. 


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Chip details
12-core CPU and 12-core GPU in the existing M6 Mac mini
TSMC 2nm manufacturing process
Up to 170GB/s memory bandwidth
Improved AI processing with Neural Accelerators

				
					

				
			
The M6 chip is expected to incorporate new features for improved AI processing.

Apple




Apple has introduced the M6 chip in the Mac mini, giving us a clear idea of what to expect from the upcoming MacBook Pro. The M6 is Apple’s first M-series chip built using TSMC’s 2nm manufacturing process, bringing improvements to CPU, GPU, and AI performance.
The M6 in the Mac mini features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, up from the M5’s 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU. It also introduces Neural Accelerators in every GPU core and a dual 16-core Neural Engine, boosting performance in AI workloads. The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to benefit from the same architectural improvements, making it particularly appealing to users running AI-powered applications and local AI models.
The Mac mini also provides an indication of what to expect from memory bandwidth. Earlier rumors suggested the M6 could reach 200GB/s, but the M6 Mac mini delivers up to 170GB/s with 24GB or 32GB of unified memory. The 16GB configuration offers 153GB/s, matching the M5. This relatively modest increase could limit the performance gains delivered by the redesigned GPU.
Our analysis suggests that the additional GPU cores, higher clock speeds, and architectural improvements help the M6 deliver gains of 20 percent or more in 3D graphics performance. However, memory bandwidth limitations mean those gains aren’t as substantial as the additional processing power might suggest.
The MacBook Pro’s exact M6 specifications remain unconfirmed, but the Mac mini offers a useful preview of the chip’s capabilities. The key question is whether Apple will make further changes to the processor or memory configurations when it brings the M6 to the MacBook Pro.


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Other specifications and features
Existing 14-inch design expected; no OLED or touchscreen
The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to retain the existing 14-inch design, with few changes beyond the processor upgrade. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the display, chassis, and other hardware are likely to remain substantially unchanged from the M5 MacBook Pro.
That means buyers shouldn’t expect an OLED display or touchscreen on the standard M6 model. Those features are reportedly reserved for Apple’s redesigned premium MacBook Pro models, which are also expected to debut on October 27.

				
					

				
			
The M6 MacBook Pro could be the last entry-level model of this particular design.

Foundry




How is the M6 MacBook Pro different from the touchscreen MacBook Pro?
Apple is reportedly preparing two very different MacBook Pro updates for October 27.
The standard 14-inch MacBook Pro will move from the M5 to the M6 processor while retaining its familiar design. It should appeal to buyers who want the newer chip but don’t need a redesigned laptop.
The higher-end MacBook Pro models, meanwhile, are expected to introduce an OLED touchscreen, a thinner and lighter chassis, and potentially an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout. Despite these upgrades, the redesigned models will reportedly use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than M6 Pro and M6 Max processors.
This reflects Apple’s reported decision to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation and focus development resources on the M7 family, which is expected in 2027.
Although the standard M6 is a newer chip, the M5 Pro and M5 Max are designed for more demanding professional workloads, so buyers shouldn’t assume the M6 MacBook Pro will be the more powerful option. It’s a similar situation to the Mac mini lineup, where the standard model features the M6 chip while the higher-end configuration uses the M5 Pro. 
The choice could therefore come down to whether buyers prioritize the latest chip at a lower price or a more powerful MacBook Pro with a redesigned display and chassis.


						

							






FeatureM6 MacBook ProOLED touchscreen MacBook Pro

Expected announcementOctober 27, 2026October 27, 2026
ProcessorM6M5 Pro / M5 Max
Screen sizes14-inchPremium MacBook Pro sizes; expected 14- and 16-inch
DisplayExisting non-OLED displayOLED
TouchscreenNoYes
DesignExisting chassisThinner, lighter redesign
PriceFrom around $1,999Higher pricing expected/

 






M6 MacBook Pro: Price
$1,999/£1,999 starting price possible
We haven’t heard any reports about the price of the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro, but we can look at recent price history to get an idea. When the M5 MacBook Pro was released in 2025, its starting price was $1,599. Apple bumped it to $1,699 when the M5 Pro and Max models arrived earlier this year and increased the starting storage to 1TB. This past June, however, Apple raised the price to $1,999 due to supply chain constraints. Those constraints aren’t going away anytime soon, and it’s likely that the higher price is now the new normal.
During Apple’s Q3 2026 financial announcement in July, Apple CEO Tim Cook and CFO Kevan Parekh made it a point to explain that the supply chain constraints will affect production costs for months to come. ” We expect the impact from supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially,” said Parekh. “The projected supply constraints in the September quarter affect iPhone, Mac, and iPad.” Cook said, “With less flexibility in supply chain, we expect the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially.”
The existing M5 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999/£1,999, following the price increases introduced in June 2026, and the M6 could retain that starting price.
However, another price increase is possible. Ongoing memory and storage shortages continue to affect Apple’s manufacturing costs, and the company may need to pass some of those costs on to buyers.
The redesigned OLED touchscreen models are also expected to carry a premium over the existing MacBook Pro lineup, making the standard M6 a potentially more affordable alternative for buyers who want a new MacBook Pro without paying extra for the redesigned display and chassis.


						

							


Should you wait for the M6 MacBook Pro?
With Apple reportedly planning to announce the M6 MacBook Pro on October 27, there’s a strong argument for waiting before buying a new 14-inch MacBook Pro. The announcement is expected in just a few weeks, and it should provide clarity on performance, pricing, and availability.
Wait for the M6 MacBook Pro if: You’re planning to buy the standard 14-inch MacBook Pro and don’t urgently need a new laptop. The M6 should provide improved CPU, GPU, and AI performance over the M5, without requiring a move to Apple’s more expensive Pro and Max models.
Consider the OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro if: You’re interested in a more substantial upgrade, particularly the rumored touchscreen display, OLED technology, and thinner design. Those models are expected to continue using M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, making them potentially better choices for demanding professional workloads.
Buy an M5 MacBook Pro now if: You need a laptop immediately or find a substantial discount. The existing M5, M5 Pro, and M5 Max MacBook Pro models remain capable machines, and a reduced price could make them better value than a newly launched M6 model.
Wait for the M7 MacBook Pro if: You’re particularly interested in OLED but don’t need the touchscreen. Reports suggest Apple’s entry-level MacBook Pro could adopt the redesigned OLED chassis in 2027 with an M7 processor, although the timing remains uncertain.
For most people considering the entry-level MacBook Pro, waiting until October 27 makes sense. Even if the M6 doesn’t offer enough of an improvement to justify its price, its arrival could create opportunities to buy the outgoing M5 model at a discount.

This is a good-looking 3-in-1 charging stand for your iPhone, Watch, and AirPods case. For each device, it’s as fast as they come, and an (albeit audible) cooling fan can be switched on for the speediest charging results.

What is it? A premium 3-in-1 Qi2 wireless charging stand with active cooling and a built-in power display.
Who is it best for? iPhone, Apple Watch and AirPods owners who want a stylish desktop charger with fast wireless charging and detailed power information.
Who should skip it? Light sleepers, frequent travelers and users who don’t need active cooling or a charging display.
Ugreen’s MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Magnetic Wireless Charging Stand 25W looks different to most wireless charging stands on the market. It’s not a classic charging tree design like the Anker Prime 3-in-1 MagGo Charging Station or Belkin BoostCharge Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand, nor a squat stand, flat pod, or cube.
It closely resembles a modern-day reimagining of the old-style Shure Elvis microphone, with its large silver circular iPhone-charging module ringed with air vents on the sides and a large fan at the rear. It’s not shy of being a statement piece on your desk or nightstand, or frightened to show off its iPhone cooling tech. The iPhone charging module can tilt more than 90 degrees. The Watch module can lie flat or be raised for Nightstand Mode.
How fast does the MagFlow Pro charge each device?
iPhone: up to 25W (iPhone 16 and later); 15W (earlier iPhones)
Apple Watch: 5W
AirPods case: 5W
Those specs mean it should fast-charge each device, although speeds will decrease when all three are used simultaneously—with a maximum output of 32.5W. It ships with its own 45W wall charger so is well covered by that. Although the MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 doesn’t include a spare USB-C port itself—look to Mophie’s StealthCharge 4-in-1 Charging Stand for extra ports and cables—you could simply use the Ugreen wall charger for your MacBook, although not as speedily as the iPhone, Watch, or AirPods.
If 25W charging can be sustained, an iPhone could reach 50% in around 30 minutes; 45 minutes at 15W.
An Apple Watch, such as the Series 11, should charge from 0-50% in about 20 minutes.
(We use the 0-50% measurement as batteries charge slower as they get fuller, so the first 50% of a charge is the best comparison when testing different units.)

				
					

				
			The fan at the back of the MagFlow Pro is the largest we’ve seen on any wireless charger.
Simon Jary




How does the MagFlow Pro stay cool?
All that high-powered charging generates heat, especially for the iPhone that can reach 25W for iPhones 16 and later (15W for earlier iPhones).
Most gadgets don’t like hot temperatures that can damage battery life and the iPhone has built-in safeguards that throttle the incoming power if it feels that it’s getting too warm. That means the 25W might be slowed to 15W or less, and even turned off until the phone cools down by itself.
To reduce the threat of the iPhone dialling back the power and therefore the charging speed, Ugreen employs active cooling via the built-in fan. Ugreen calls the 15dB fan “ultra quiet” but you can hear it humming with a rushing wind sound. True, it’s nothing like setting off a hair dryer but it’s definitely audible.
When you’re not in a rush to charge your iPhone, you can turn the cooling fan off with one of the easy-access side buttons (see below). This is certainly recommended if charging by your bedside at night, unless you’re a white-noise enthusiast. Charging overnight doesn’t require the highest speed anyway, so there’s no need for the fan as the iPhone will take in power as it feels fit while you sleep or while you’re working at your desk. But you can turn on the cooling blaster when you’re in a real hurry for power.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




What does the MagFlow’s display show?
There’s a trend for chargers and charging stands to include a real-time display, and the MagFlow Pro’s display is on the front of the arm that suspends the iPhone charger.
The TFT display shows charging wattage for each device, charging surface temperature, and cooling mode. Along the side of the arm are two buttons that you use to switch off the charger and its cooling mode, plus switch from one info-screen to another.
I’m not sure many people other than gadget geeks and tech reviewers—quite the Venn diagram—are going to pay much attention to such in-depth charging data, but it’s handy if you’re a power data control freak.

				
					

				
			The MagFlow Pro’s Apple Watch charging module can lay flat when not in use, and be raised to work in Nightstand Mode.
Simon Jary




What’s it like to use every day?
The MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand is an attractive elevated charging stand for a desk or nightstand with tilting iPhone-charging pad, a non-slip AirPods case charging module at the front, and an adjustable Apple Watch charger sat at the back.
It has a small footprint, with a 4.6-inch (117mm) base diameter. It weighs 19.1oz (541g). Charging stands require a decent heft to stay stable. If you want a more portable 3-in-1 travel charger, consider the Anker MagGo 3-in-1 Folding Wireless Charging Station, Kuxiu X40 Turbo 25W Wireless Charging Stand, or ESR CryoBoost Foldable 3-in-1 Magnetic Charging Station. Ugreen’s own $59 / £43 MagFlow 2-in-1 Foldable Magnetic Wireless Charger is also worth considering but lacks the Watch charger found on the other travel charger.

				
					

				
			iPhone shown in Decoded Silicone Case; Apple Watch with UNIQ Revix IV PANTONE Edition Reversible Apple Watch Band. 
Simon Jary




How much does the Ugreen MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 cost?
The Ugreen MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand is priced at $159.95 / £119.99 direct or on Amazon / Amazon UK.
Check out our reviews of the best wireless charging stations for alternatives, although if you admire this form factor there’s nothing really to stop you ordering one right away.
Should you buy the MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand 25W?
The Ugreen MagFlow Pro is an attractive, well-built charging stand that brings together fast Qi2 wireless charging, adjustable iPhone and Apple Watch charging pads, and a useful display showing real-time power consumption and temperature.
Its standout feature is the built-in cooling fan, designed to help prevent heat from slowing iPhone charging. However, the fan is noticeably audible, which makes the MagFlow Pro better suited to a desk than a quiet bedside table.
At $159.95/£119.99, it’s a premium option, and cheaper 3-in-1 chargers will meet the needs of users who simply want to charge their Apple devices overnight. But if you value its distinctive design, cooling system and detailed charging information, the MagFlow Pro has plenty to offer.

title: How the new Apple Watch sensors affect battery life
content:
Macworld





Apple has radically overhauled the fundamentals of health tracking with the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. They have new sensors that are larger and take readings more frequently. During the day, the Series 12 and Ultra 4 measure heart rate every five seconds instead of every five minutes. Heart rate variability is also measured more frequently: every five minutes instead of every two hours.
With this increase in frequency, is battery life affected? We tested how this background activity affects the Apple Watch’s battery life. Do you need to worry about battery life, and should you definitely carry a suitable power bank with you?
To find the answers to these questions, I wore an Apple Watch Series 11 on my left wrist and the Apple Watch Series 12 on my right wrist, and analyzed the data from a seven-hour hike. The first half was spent in power-saving mode, the second half in normal workout mode. After the hike, both watches were left running in the background to measure my heart rate, display notifications, and show the time.
The following day, I exported and analyzed the telemetry data from both watches. WatchOS collects telemetry data at 15-minute intervals–in this test, that means that 60 data points were collected for the day (from 8 a.m. to 11 p.m.). A single day does not allow for any general conclusions about battery consumption, but it can indicate a trend.
Whether in power-saving mode or not, an Apple Watch runs continuously in the background during a workout. Both Apple Watches, Series 11 and 12, consistently recorded 900 seconds of background activity per 15 minutes; the power-saving mode setting had no effect on this. What does switch off, however, is the display. On average, it lights up much less frequently in power-saving mode, thereby conserving battery life.
As the energy capacity of each Apple Watch is known in watt-hours and the Battery system setting displays the percentage of maximum capacity, it is possible to calculate how much energy each Apple Watch can consume per hour and per quarter of an hour.
With the new Apple Watch Series 12, which has a 1.461 watt-hour battery and 100 percent of its maximum capacity, 14.61 milliwatt-hours of energy are consumed for every one percent of battery charge. With our Apple Watch Series 11, which has a 1.403 watt-hour battery and 98 percent of its maximum capacity, 13.74 milliwatt-hours are consumed per one percent of the battery charge.

		
			


The overall power consumption chart clearly shows that the two Apple Watches are on a par in power-saving mode. Background activities on both watches are running at full speed, while the display brightness is reduced to a minimum. It is only after power-saving mode is switched off that battery consumption increases on the Apple Watch Series 11. This is because, during that period, it was the actively paired watch and therefore had to deliver notifications and push alerts from the iPhone. The Series 12 was unpaired from the iPhone and did not have to perform these tasks.

		
			


It is also interesting to look at the period after the workout. This is the point that Apple particularly emphasised during the keynote: the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 measure health data significantly more frequently throughout the day. Between 5:30 p.m. and 11 p.m., the Apple Watch Series 11 recorded 4,222 seconds (70 minutes) of background activity, while the Series 12 recorded 4,883 seconds (81 minutes) of background activity. On average, therefore, the Series 11 is active in the background for 13 minutes per hour, while the Series 12 is active for 15 minutes per hour.
Despite the longer period of background activity, the energy consumption of the two smartwatches differs only slightly. During this period, our Series 11 consumed around 0.248 Wh, while the Series 12 consumed around 0.190 Wh; this difference can be explained by slightly more intensive use of the display on the Apple Watch Series 11.

		
			


Even with the more frequent background monitoring of health data, there is no need to worry about the battery life of the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. The system is designed to be energy-efficient, so the more intensive heart rate monitoring does not result in increased energy consumption. You can confidently make the most of the Apple Watch’s new health features and look for power-hungry components in other areas, such as the display.

title: Apple 'Welcome Home' Launch: Everything to Expect Tomorrow
content:
Apple's "Welcome Home" product launch is happening tomorrow. As the name suggests, Apple is going to debut new home accessories, including the long-rumored home hub.


Below, we've listed all the rumors we know about the three devices Apple is set to introduce.

HomeView

Apple's home hub, which will be called HomeView, is a multi-function device designed for all of a home's occupants. It's built around Siri AI, and will have an A18 chip and 8GB of RAM.


Here's what rumors suggest it'll be able to do:

 
Answer questions with ‌Siri‌ AI

 
Control smart home devices

 
Display the time and weather

 
Display widgets, including widgets from a connected iPhone

 
Show each user their calendar events and reminders

 
Play music, podcasts, and audiobooks

 
Play videos, TV shows, and movies

 
Show photos, slideshows, and home movies

 
Support video calls

 
Show the news

 
Show messages and emails

 
Display recipes and instructions when completing tasks


The hub will be able to do anything you might want a home assistant device to do, from giving the next steps of a recipe to suggesting dinner ideas and creating a shopping list. It will rely heavily on ‌Siri‌ AI for voice-based input, but it will also have a 6-inch touch display.

App Store, but it will support Apple apps such as Safari, News, Music, Reminders, Calendar, Weather, Messages, FaceTime, Photos, and Mail.

Face ID to determine who is nearby to show customized content. It will display information from a linked iPhone, like email messages, but only after authenticating. The sensors in the hub will be usable in HomeKit scenes and automations, so you can use it to trigger lights and other devices when a person walks into the room. 

HomePod mini. 

There isn't going to be a built-in battery, and the hub will need to be connected to power via an included USB-C port. The speaker-equipped version is expected in multiple colors, including gray, silver, starlight, and rose. The wall-mounted version will be available in silver and gray.

Rumors suggest the hub could be priced somewhere around $350.

Apple TV 4K

Apple isn't updating the design of the Apple TV, so expect the new model to be the same boring black box. What's changing is entirely inside.


The ‌Apple TV‌ 4K is going to get a lot more powerful so it can support ‌Siri‌ AI, offering many of the same ‌Siri‌ features that are available on iPhone and iPad in iOS and iPadOS 27.

We're expecting an A19 with 8GB of RAM, along with Apple's N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. The A19 will bring a major upgrade in performance, both for ‌Siri‌ and for gaming. It has ray tracing, mesh shading, and other features that will improve gameplay graphics.

gaming controller under the Beats brand, but there's no word on whether it's ready to launch.

Apple will likely emphasize ‌Siri‌ AI and gaming capabilities when introducing the ‌Apple TV‌. Apple raised the price of the current ‌Apple TV‌ to $199 in June, and the new model will be at least that expensive with the processor and RAM upgrades.

HomePod mini

Like the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K, the ‌HomePod mini‌ isn't going to get a new design, but it will have internal upgrades that make it more capable. It's going to get an upgraded S10 chip, second-generation UWB for features like Handoff, and the N1 networking chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.


You'll need a nearby AI-capable device for ‌Siri‌ AI processing because the HomePod probably won't be able to handle much on-device, but smarter ‌Siri‌ should make for a better experience. ‌Siri‌ AI on ‌HomePod mini‌ will have the context of ‌Siri‌ interactions on other devices, and it's likely conversations will be saved to a connected iPhone's ‌Siri‌ app.

‌Siri‌ AI can answer follow-up questions, handle multi-request queries, and access information from your apps. It'll be similar to having ChatGPT or Claude on a speaker. Though design updates aren't expected, the ‌HomePod mini‌ will get new colors. We're expecting white, blue, black, sage, and pink.

‌HomePod mini‌ pricing went up from $99 to $129 in June 2026, and the new model will likely be priced at $129 too.

LG Accessories

Apple worked with LG to make an LG-branded wired video doorbell, thermostat, smart deadbolt lock, temperature sensor, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera, and floodlight camera that will work with the home hub and the ‌HomeKit‌ platform.

The accessories are part of an "Apple Home Collection" that will be marketed alongside the HomeView. They won't be ready until later this year at the earliest, but Apple could show them off during the announcement. 

Announcement Timing

There's no keynote event for the "Welcome Home" product debut, so Apple is probably going to release a video and an accompanying set of press releases. There's an NYC media event that's going to take place at 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday, October 13, and that could be when all of the announcements happen.

The NYC event will let members of the media get some hands-on time with the new devices to share first impressions.

Pre-Orders and Launch Date

Apple could begin accepting pre-orders just after the new devices launch. The ‌HomePod mini‌ and the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K are going to launch on Friday, October 30.

title: Apple and Pokémon Tease Special Pikachu-Themed Beats Pill Speaker
content:
Beats today shared a short video teasing a new collaboration with Pokémon, and it appears this will be for a Pikachu-themed Beats Pill speaker.


"Time to catch something new," the video title says. The short clip shows a Beats Pill speaker and Beats and Poké Ball icons side by side.

BritBratTV shared two photos of an alleged Pikachu-themed Beats Pill speaker box at U.S. retailer Target, so that is likely what this teaser video is for. A release date has yet to be disclosed.



Apple re-released the Beats Pill in 2024, after discontinuing the previous version in 2022. In the U.S., the Bluetooth speaker is regularly priced at $149.99.

visited Apple Park in August.

Is free antivirus for Mac good enough?
Free antivirus software can provide basic protection, but it often lacks advanced features such as ransomware protection, firewalls and real-time web security. Paid options offer more comprehensive, all-round protection.
Apple includes built-in security tools like XProtect and Gatekeeper, which block known malware and unverified apps. However, in our testing, it was still possible to install Mac malware or suspicious software if warnings were ignored, showing that Apple’s protections alone are not foolproof.
Free third-party antivirus tools offer an advantage in that they are updated more frequently and can protect against a wider range of threats, including adware, spyware, trojans and ransomware.
The core antivirus engine is often the same in both free and paid versions. The difference lies in the extra features included in premium suites, such as web and phishing protection, VPNs, identity monitoring, parental controls and customer support.
Ultimately, you get what you pay for. If security is a priority, a paid antivirus offers the most complete protection. However, if you’re on a tight budget, a free antivirus is still better than relying solely on Apple’s built-in security tools.
If you’re on a really tight budget, a free antivirus is still going to do a better job of protecting you than Apple’s security tools. For some low-priced AV options, check out the best Mac antivirus deals for the best prices.

Our recommendations are based on a combination of independent lab data, structured testing and real-world usage – not just specifications or vendor claims. We regularly review and update our rankings to reflect the latest threats, software updates and performance improvements.
How we test Mac antivirus software
To identify the best antivirus software for Mac, we combine hands-on testing, real-world threat simulation and independent lab data. Our goal is to assess how effectively each product protects your Mac without compromising performance, usability or value.
Real-world testing environment: We begin with a clean installation of macOS, which is then cloned for each antivirus product. Each app is installed and tested in isolation to ensure results are not affected by other software — particularly important as antivirus tools can sometimes flag each other as threats. 
We simulate real-world attack scenarios by:
Downloading known malware samples
Visiting malicious and phishing websites
Testing suspicious files and drive-by downloads
Running malware in controlled conditions
This allows us to evaluate how well each product detects and blocks both online and offline threats, including Mac-specific malware, adware and potentially unwanted programs (PUPs). We also assess how effectively each tool detects and handles Windows-based malware, which can still pose a risk when sharing files.
Independent lab validation: To support our findings, we reference results from leading independent testing organisations:
AV-Test
AV-Comparatives
These labs evaluate antivirus software against large sets of known malware and potentially unwanted applications, measuring detection rates, false positives and overall protection. Where lab data is unavailable, we carry out more extensive in-house testing using real malware samples.
Performance impact: Antivirus software should protect your Mac without slowing it down. We measure performance by assessing:
System responsiveness during full and quick scans
Impact of real-time protection on everyday tasks
Background CPU and resource usage
We prioritise solutions that deliver strong protection with minimal noticeable slowdown, since overly demanding software is more likely to be disabled by users.
Features, usability and user experience: We spend time using each product to evaluate how intuitive and practical it is in daily use. This includes:
Ease of installation and setup
Interface design and macOS integration
Clarity and relevance of alerts and notifications
We also assess additional features, including:
Ransomware protection
Web and phishing protection
Firewalls and network monitoring
VPNs and privacy tools
Password managers and parental controls
Importantly, we consider whether these features are genuinely useful or simply added complexity.
Value for money: We evaluate pricing and overall value, including:
Subscription costs and renewal pricing
Number of devices covered
Features included at each tier
Our focus is on products that offer a strong balance of protection, performance and features at a reasonable price.


						

							




Should I get an antivirus for my Mac? 


ScenarioRecommendation

Low-risk user (App Store only, trusted devs, automatic updates on)Apple’s built-in tools are sufficient.
High-risk user (downloads from various sites, torrents, handles sensitive data)Paid antivirus is strongly recommended.
Business user (handles client data, shares files with Windows PCs)Paid antivirus is recommended for an extra safety layer.
User wanting extra features (VPN, password manager, phishing protection)Paid antivirus is worthwhile for the bundled features.

 




 Best Mac Antivirus: FAQ 


1.
Do Macs need antivirus software?
Yes – while Macs are generally more secure than Windows PCs and include built-in protections like XProtect and sandboxing, which helps limit how far malware can spread, these measures are not enough to defend against modern threats such as phishing, adware and ransomware. 
Adding a dedicated antivirus tool helps close those gaps, provides broader coverage against evolving threats and extra layer of security when browsing the web or downloading files.
For more detail, see our guide to whether Macs need antivirus, along with our Mac security tips and advice on how to remove a virus from a Mac.
Do iPhones need antivirus software? 
You may be considering a Mac Antivirus that also offers to protect your iPhone, but is that protection really necessary? 
Apple’s iOS is designed with strong built-in security, including app sandboxing, strict App Store review processes and system-level protections that prevent traditional viruses from infecting your device. This makes it very difficult for malware to spread in the same way it can on other platforms. So, no – iPhones generally don’t need antivirus software.
However, iPhones are not completely risk-free. Threats like phishing attacks, malicious websites and data breaches can still affect users. Instead of installing an antivirus app the best advice is to keep iOS up to date, avoid clicking on suspicious links, use strong passwords and two-factor authentication, and don’t download anything unless you are sure it is safe. 





2.
How does antivirus software protect your Mac?
Mac antivirus software protects your device using a combination of on-demand scans and real-time (always-on) protection.
On-demand scanning checks files when you run a manual or scheduled scan. This can take time, especially on systems with lots of data, and may temporarily use more system resources. For best results, scans are often scheduled to run at convenient times. See how to scan a Mac for malware
Real-time protection works continuously in the background. If malware arrives – for example via an email attachment or downloaded file – the antivirus can detect and block it immediately. Suspicious files are typically quarantined, meaning they are moved to a secure location where they can’t cause harm while you decide whether to delete or restore them.
The effectiveness of these two layers of protection is the most important factor when choosing antivirus software, but additional features can also make a difference.
Many Mac antivirus tools now include ransomware protection, which prevents unauthorised apps from accessing sensitive folders such as Documents or Photos. Only trusted apps are allowed access, and you can customise these permissions.
Web protection is another key feature, often delivered via browser extensions. This helps block malicious websites, phishing attempts and unsafe downloads, reducing the risk of accidentally exposing personal information.





3.
Should my Mac antivirus include a VPN?
Yes, a VPN can be a useful addition to Mac antivirus software. It encrypts your internet connection, helping protect your data – especially on public Wi-Fi. However, built-in VPNs are often limited, so a dedicated VPN service usually offers better performance and features.
Some Mac antivirus packages include a built-in VPN (virtual private network), although VPNs are also widely available as standalone products. For many users, VPNs are appealing because they can mask your location and allow access to region-restricted content, such as streaming services.
More importantly, a VPN improves security by encrypting your internet connection, which is particularly useful when using public Wi-Fi networks. This helps protect your data from interception and reduces the risk of cyberattacks.
While we generally recommend a dedicated Mac VPN service for the best performance and features, a VPN included with antivirus software can still be a useful extra. Just be aware that bundled VPNs often come with limitations, such as data caps or reduced functionality, and may prompt you to upgrade to a full subscription.





4.
What is the best value Mac antivirus?
Value means different things to different users. For some, it’s the best free option; for others, it’s a reasonably priced product with the most useful features. We define value as the best overall balance of protection, performance and features – and for protecting a single Mac, we believe Intego offers the best value.
That said, there are ways to save money on even the top antivirus products. Most Mac antivirus apps are sold as annual subscriptions, often with significant discounts for the first year. When that period ends, you can switch providers to take advantage of new introductory offers, or opt for longer-term plans (such as two- or three-year subscriptions) to reduce the overall cost.
Many antivirus suites also cover multiple devices, including Windows PCs and Android smartphones. If you have several devices in your household, a multi-device plan can offer excellent value. 
For the latest offers, see our guide to the Best Mac Antivirus deals, which includes the most affordable options.





5.
How to spot fake Mac antivirus software?
Because many of us are waking up to the idea that malware is a threat to the Mac, malware writers have made it their business to play on that fear. There have been cases of malware writers disguising their viruses as antivirus apps – two notable examples are Mac Auto Fixer and MacDefender. It’s important to always read reviews on reputable sites such as Macworld before installing any software on your Mac or MacBook.
At the same time, don’t believe everything you read. MacKeeper is a great example of an antivirus program that has got a bad rap, but it’s worked hard to repair its reputation. It has gained Apple Notarization, which means the software has been checked by Apple for malicious components, and the company has garnering certification from various bodies to prove it isn’t a PUP (potentially unwanted program), including an AV-Test certificate. That said, we haven’t recommended it here, and that’s simply because we feel that there are better options available. If you have already installed MacKeeper and wish to try one of our alternative recommendations, we explain How to uninstall MacKeeper.





6.
What can’t Mac antivirus protect you from?
Using a Mac antivirus product, especially one that includes tools to improve your online privacy, may lull you into believing you’re completely safe from personal and private information leaking out and that you no longer need to keep your wits about you. That’s not quite the case. While there’s no reason to panic, you should still practice caution – and there are a few more issues you should consider when using Mac antivirus, too.
First, an antivirus for Mac product may upload the complete text of files flagged to the cloud, where it can be analyzed by separate tools hosted there. This practice is normal and sensible: some malware can detect when a running process may examine it, and will then engage in subterfuge. Antivirus software makers also can access their massive databases to examine files with characteristics that trigger their algorithms – certain elements that match known malware. As a result, security researchers discover new viruses, worms, Trojans horses, and the like. However, helping the greater good means you’ll have to be comfortable with trusting a third-party with your file contents. Where appropriate, we noted privacy policy issues in individual reviews.
Second, this software may also rely partly or entirely on cloud-based checks of URLs, malware, and the like. Accordingly, an antivirus package might upload every URL you visit, metadata about files, signatures of files, information about your computer’s hardware, a list of running or installed applications, and more. Companies vary on their disclosure of such policies, and may not let you opt out of this kind of sharing. We note issues in each review as appropriate.
Third, antivirus software makers also get a sense of what behavior is happening on your computer that’s being monitored or blocked, and may use that information for their own purposes. In some cases, you can opt out of this information gathering.





7.
What virus cleaner does Apple recommend?
Apple has never recommended a third-party virus cleaner, and has instead focused on the Xprotect and Gatekeeper functions found within macOS, which are regularly updated with operating system updates.





8.
How good is Apple’s virus protection?
It’s actually very good, and there isn’t much that gets past it in the way of viruses and malware, given its Xprotect and Gatekeeper features – but these can be overridden, and questionable software can be installed and activated if the user knows what they’re doing.
Still, the protection is present, it’s updated well, and Apple keeps a good eye on things, but new viruses and malware are sent out from bad actors all the time, and this is where a good third-party application can come in handy.
We have tested Apple’s own solution against a range of malware samples. While it did a reasonable job overall, we found instances where questionable applications could be installed without any warning. A helpful analogy is to think of Apple’s built-in antivirus system, XProtect, as the lock on your Mac’s front door, while a paid antivirus solution acts more like an alarm system with security cameras. Third-party tools update their virus definitions – including not just viruses, but also adware, spyware, trojans, and ransomware – several times a day, often more frequently than Apple’s protections, providing real-time defense against new and emerging threats.
During our testing of Apple’s malware protections, recovery options were limited. In some cases, the only solution was to wipe the Mac and restore from a backup made before the risky behavior – hoping nothing had already spread. Apple does not offer dedicated malware removal support or guarantees if an infection occurs, nor does it protect against cross-platform threats across multiple devices. Paid antivirus software typically includes these services, along with additional features such as web and phishing protection, vulnerability patching tools, VPNs, password managers, parental controls, secure cloud backup, and dark web monitoring.
That said, macOS’s built-in security may be sufficient for low-risk users who install apps only from the App Store or trusted developers, keep automatic updates enabled, avoid pirated software, do not disable Gatekeeper, have limited exposure to risky email attachments, and do not handle sensitive client data.
Ultimately, investing in a reputable security suite for Mac adds an extra layer of protection – and for many users, it’s a case of being safe rather than sorry.





9.
Is there free virus protection for Mac?
The Xprotect and Gatekeeper functions serve as free virus protection for macOS, but you can also get basic virus protection from many of the well-known antivirus providers, we have some recommendations above. 





10.
How to choose the best Mac antivirus for your needs
There are a lot of Mac antivirus programs to choose from. What you want is one that offers a familiar and easy-to-use interface that works well on a Mac – a key reason why we recommend Intego’s antivirus. You should also look for antivirus with a good detection rate – not just for Mac viruses, but also for PC viruses, unless you want to be passing viruses on to friends and clients running Windows. Low impact on system resources is also critical, especially if your Mac isn’t the most powerful model.
Consider the type and number of devices you want to protect – are you looking for an app to cover one Mac, or Mac, iPhone, iPad and even a PC? Your budget matters here, too: do you prefer a subscription model or a one-time payment?
Mac antivirus vendors typically offer different add-ons, and it is certainly a case of you get what you pay for: free products will have fewer bells and whistles, but the most comprehensive Mac security suites will include password managers, parental controls, cloud storage and more. The underlying antimalware engine will usually be the same for all security products from a particular company, so you can save money if you don’t need all those extra features.





11.
When are Apple’s built-in protections sufficient
For many users, Apple’s layered security – XProtect, Gatekeeper and Rapid Security Responses – is more than adequate. If you fit into the “low-risk” category described below, you can probably rely on macOS alone.
You only download apps from the Mac App Store or trusted developers. Gatekeeper ensures that only notarized software from identified developers can run, and XProtect scans these apps for known malware on launch.
You keep automatic updates enabled. Apple regularly updates XProtect’s malware definitions in the background, and with macOS Tahoe, Background Security Improvements can now install critical patches silently without requiring a restart.
You avoid pirated software, torrents, and “cracks.” These are common vectors for malware that can bypass Apple’s checks if a user overrides warnings. 
You do not handle sensitive client data or work in a high-risk environment. For casual home use, the built-in tools are generally enough to block the most obvious threats





12.
When paid Antivirus is worthwhile
Despite Apple’s strong foundation, there are clear gaps that third-party software fills.
You frequently install software from various internet sources. In our hands-on testing, we have found that it is still possible to install malware by ignoring or bypassing Gatekeeper warnings. Our testers were able to install trojans, fake apps, and software that requested access to the microphone, webcam, and keystrokes.
You want protection against phishing and malicious websites. Apple’s XProtect primarily focuses on known malware files. It does not offer the same level of real-time web and phishing protection that suites like Avast One or Bitdefender provide.
You need more frequent updates and broader threat coverage. Third-party tools update their virus definitions several times a day, often more frequently than Apple’s updates. They also cover a wider range of threats, including adware, spyware, trojans, and ransomware.
You want features like a firewall, VPN, password manager, or identity monitoring. Apple does not offer a dedicated, configurable firewall for macOS (it relies on the built-in one) and does not include a VPN, password manager, or dark web monitoring in its security suite. Paid suites bundle these features.
You share files with Windows users. An unprotected Mac can unknowingly harbor Windows viruses that won’t affect macOS but can be passed on to friends and colleagues. A good antivirus will detect and clean cross-platform threats.

title: You Can Now Set Up Your iPhone Duo Pre-Order - Do It Before Friday
content:
Apple has opened its "Get Ready" service for iPhone Duo pre-orders, allowing customers to pre-select a variety of options to streamline the process of ordering and have a better chance of grabbing one on launch day.


The iPhone Duo launches on October 23, while pre-orders go live on October 16 at 5 a.m. Pacific Time or 8 a.m. Eastern Time. Rather than turn up on the day, however, Apple encourages customers to take action before then and increase the chances of securing their preferred model on day one of sales.

Apple's online store and in its Apple Store app, and it lets you select a preferred color and capacity ahead of time. It also lets you confirm your carrier status, choose your accessories, pick an AppleCare+ plan, select a trade-in, add a payment method, and set a shipping and billing address.

Get Ready is really helpful because when pre-orders go live, it allows you to essentially perform a one-tap order. That's a real advantage when it comes to iPhone Duo, given that supplies are expected to be limited. 

It's been said before about other iPhones, but pre-orders of the iPhone Duo really could sell out within minutes – there have been multiple reports of production issues leading to supply constraints, and users who have completed Get Ready will be able to submit orders faster.

title: Avira Prime for Mac review: Strong malware protection and useful cleanup tools
content:
Macworld





At a Glance
Expert's Rating



Pros
Strong core malware protection

Inconvenient cookie searching and scan logs
Our Verdict 
Avira Prime offers strong Mac malware protection, excellent scanning and scheduling, and useful cleanup tools. However, its VPN lacks advanced features, Identity Assistant failed during testing, and some malware components were left behind. Despite these shortcomings, it’s a capable security suite worth trying during its 30-day trial.
