What is it: Avira Prime is a comprehensive Mac security suite combining antivirus and malware protection with a VPN, password manager, privacy features, and useful cleanup and system-maintenance tools.
Who is it best for: Mac users looking for a comprehensive security suite that combines antivirus protection with useful cleanup, application-removal, and system-maintenance tools.
Who should skip it: Users who need advanced VPN capabilities, detailed security reporting, or dependable identity-monitoring features may find that Avira Prime doesn’t go far enough.
At a glance
Protection: ★★★★☆
Performance: ★★★★☆
Features: ★★★★☆
Ease of use: ★★★★☆
Value: ★★★★☆
There are times when the focus seems right, the execution doesn’t quite match, but there’s still a good utility to be had anyway. Enter Avira Prime, the security and utility suite from longtime developer Avira, which now stands at version 2.3.10 and has been dubbed “Avira Security” at the application level.
Available for macOS 10.15 (Catalina) or later, the latest version combines antivirus and malware protection with a VPN, password manager, privacy features, and a range of cleanup tools. Testing on a MacBook Pro running macOS Tahoe 26.6.2 revealed strong core protection, an impressive scanning interface, and some genuinely useful utilities, alongside a few missed opportunities and one feature that failed to work properly.
Features: What do you actually get?
Avira Prime breaks down into Security, Privacy, and Performance categories from the home screen. The Security category offers Virus Scans, Protection Options, and Quarantine, while the Privacy and Performance sections offer VPN, Passwords, Cookie Cleaner, Identity Assistant, Junk Cleaner, Uninstaller, and Startup Apps tools. Other features include a Status indicator, Activity history, and a Scheduler.
There’s a good set of genuinely focused tools here without going overboard, although their usefulness varies.
Malware protection

				
					

				
			Avira Prime’s Full Scan shows the files being checked, elapsed time, and estimated time remaining, making it easier to follow a lengthy malware scan.

Foundry




Antivirus and malware removal remain Avira’s bread and butter, and what’s there is impressive.
The application offers Quick, Full, and Custom Scans, with the latter allowing you to drag and drop volumes for scanning or locate specific volumes, folders, or files through the Finder. It’s a flexible approach that makes it easy to check an external drive or investigate something suspicious without having to run a complete system scan.
This combines with customizable settings for Real-time Protection, Download Protection, and USB Protection, the latter checking USB devices as they’re connected. Avira also integrates well with macOS’s built-in XProtect and Gatekeeper protection features.
The Quarantine tool displays the file paths where malware was discovered, allowing you to review the findings. Unfortunately, the lack of a convenient scan-log export function makes more detailed reporting tedious, particularly if you’re considering Avira Prime as an office systems-administration tool.
VPN and password management
Avira Prime offers VPN functionality through its Avira Phantom VPN application, and the results are something of a mixed bag.
The VPN itself performs well, offering good throughput speeds, reliable streaming, and an easy way to change geolocations as needed. The interface is straightforward, and the core functions should be enough for casual browsing and streaming.
That said, it’s a bare-bones client compared with more advanced VPN applications. Features such as port forwarding and split tunneling are limited or unavailable, and performance through peer-to-peer applications can be substantially slower. What’s present works, but users who depend on these capabilities may want to look elsewhere.
Unlimited VPN data is part of the Prime package, alongside password management and additional privacy tools, while the separate Phantom VPN application also offers a limited free allowance of 500MB per month, along with standalone subscription options. 
Like a number of its competitors, Avira is also chasing the password-management market. The Avira Password Manager extension supports Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Opera, and has you create an Avira account and a master vault password.
Once installed, it was easy enough to create a CSV file from my existing system passwords, which imported cleanly into the extension. From there, the manager activated as needed throughout my normal workday. It’s a useful addition, although anyone already committed to a separate password manager may not find much reason to switch.
Cookie Cleaner and Identity Assistant

				
					

				
			
The Cookie Cleaner lets users select cookies for removal, although the lack of a search function makes navigating large lists harder than it should be.

Foundry




The Cookie Cleaner is an interesting addition and offers tight control over cookie files, but comes with some drawbacks.
Once you’ve activated the feature and quit your open web browsers, the tool quickly scans your Mac’s cookie files. After a few minutes, it presents the dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of cookies that may be present.
The user interface is inviting, but it offers no search function for finding specific cookies, leaving you to scroll through websites and domain names displayed in a scattered, non-alphabetical order. What should be a straightforward process begins to feel like a chore, and a better way of navigating the results is needed.
Avira’s efforts towards an Identity Assistant and overall identity protection are nothing new in the current marketplace, and the feature feels more like an additional value-add than something genuinely unique.
The feature offers dark-web monitoring and allows users to provide personal information they want to track. However, it requires an additional subscription for certain levels of coverage, and the lack of a free trial for these services makes it difficult to judge their value before committing.
More importantly, the feature failed to work properly during testing. Attempts to load the initial scan and personal-information entry screen produced web-based error messages in Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Opera rather than a functioning interface.
That server-side error persisted throughout testing, making the Identity Assistant’s actual effectiveness impossible to gauge. It’s disappointing to encounter such a basic problem in a paid security suite.
Junk Cleaner, Uninstaller, and Startup Apps

				
					

				
			
Avira Prime’s Uninstaller removes an older version of Blender and its associated support files.

Foundry




Where Avira Prime’s Identity Assistant proved a stumbling block, its Junk Cleaner helped redeem the suite.
As seems to be the convention these days, the feature hunts down cache files, downloads, reports, logs, and Xcode files. On the test MacBook Pro, it offered to clean about 2.67GB of data without automatically going after everything in the Downloads folder, which would have cleared another 46.34GB.
This is backed by an elegant interface that lets you click on specific files and choose exactly which items you want to remove, rather than inadvertently targeting a large swath of data that may be unrecoverable afterwards. It’s a welcome level of control.
Avira’s Uninstaller and Startup Apps features may not be revolutionary, but they’re genuinely impressive in their simplicity.
The Uninstaller allows you to drag and drop an application onto the tool or scan your installed applications, then cleanly removes the selected software and its associated support files. It’s especially useful when you want to remove more than just the main application from the Applications folder.
The Startup Apps tool offers much the same level of control as the corresponding settings in macOS, allowing you to toggle startup items on or off. It’s a convenient addition, although it doesn’t go much further than the tools already built into the operating system.
Test results: How well does Avira Prime protect your Mac

				
					

				
			
Virus scan settings allow users to customize Avira Prime’s protection behaviour and scanning preferences.

Foundry




Antivirus and malware removal remain the strongest parts of Avira Prime, and the new version performed well in hands-on testing against more than 130 malware samples from the Objective-See Mac malware archive.
The application was able to eliminate all but a few of the samples, sometimes deleting chunks of malware as they were extracted from their archives. In these situations, it worked well alongside macOS’s built-in XProtect and Gatekeeper protections, which add their own layers of defence.
Avira Prime wasn’t completely successful, however. Elements of DevilRobber, FlexibleFerret, Lamzev, MacKeeper, notnullOSX, and SentinelSneak remained after testing.
While the software appeared to remove the executable components of some threats, it occasionally left other files behind, including developer-related files. This was worrying, although the presence of leftover files doesn’t necessarily mean that the malware remained capable of executing or causing harm.
These findings are worth bearing in mind. Avira’s core protection is impressive, but it isn’t invincible, and users should not assume that every component associated with a detected threat will necessarily be removed.
The application’s presentation of scan progress is another significant strength. A clear progress bar, elapsed time, filenames, ongoing updates, and an accurate estimated completion time make it easy to see what’s happening. This is one of the better scanning interfaces I’ve encountered in a malware utility in some time.
Independent laboratory results
Avira’s performance is also supported by independent laboratory testing.
In AV-TEST’s June 2026 assessment of Avira Security 2.3 on macOS Tahoe 26.5.1, the software achieved 6 out of 6 for protection, 6 out of 6 for performance, and 6 out of 6 for usability, earning the maximum possible overall result of 18 out of 18.
The laboratory recorded 100 percent detection of the widespread and prevalent malware in its reference set and no false positives in its reported usability tests. 
These results provide a useful independent counterpoint to the occasional leftover malware components observed during our hands-on testing. 
Performance: Will Avira Prime slow down your Mac?
Avira Prime’s scan performance proved solid, particularly when running Quick and Custom Scans.
A Quick Scan completed in just a few minutes, while a Full Scan of more than 633GB of data on the MacBook Pro’s SSD took just under three hours. Given the amount of data being scanned, the latter is the sort of task that might best be scheduled overnight or outside a busy workday.
The Custom Scan option is particularly useful because it allows you to focus on particular files, folders, or volumes rather than committing to a complete system scan every time. USB Protection offers a similarly convenient way to check removable storage as it’s connected.
The June 2026 AV-TEST results also awarded Avira Security 2.3 a maximum score for performance, suggesting that its effects on common activities, such as application launches and file copying, are generally well controlled.
Ease of use: Is it Mac-friendly?
Installation proved as easy as expected, with Avira Prime installing an endpoint security extension and requiring Full Disk Access. The application provided convenient access to macOS’s System Settings to authorize the necessary permissions.
Once configured, the main window offers easy access to the Security, Privacy, and Performance sections. The layout is inviting, with well-organized tools that are straightforward to locate and use.
The settings themselves offer finer control over virus scans, protection options, exclusions or whitelists, and the cookie and junk cleaners.
The Scheduler is particularly good, allowing you to quickly create a roster of recurring Smart Scans and Virus Scans that can be edited later. There’s no need to dig through obscure settings to create a recurring task, and the feature is impressive in its simplicity.
Finally, the Activity section provides a useful reference point for seeing which tests were performed on particular dates, helping complete the picture of your history with Avira Prime.
Not everything is quite as polished. The lack of a search function in the Cookie Cleaner makes navigating large lists unnecessarily difficult, while the limited Quarantine reporting and absence of a convenient scan-log export option become more frustrating when trying to investigate a particular threat.
Overall, though, Avira Prime offers a clean and generally approachable experience that makes its extensive collection of tools relatively easy to manage.

				
					

				
			
The Quarantine tool displays detected files and their locations, although more convenient log-export options would be welcome.

Foundry




Pricing and plans: Is Avira Prime worth the money?
Avira Prime is available as a subscription covering multiple devices across macOS, Windows, iOS, and Android, with introductory pricing that makes the suite more attractive than its longer-term renewal cost.
At the time of testing, the five-device plan was listed at $59.99/£51.99 for the first year, increasing to $109.99/£94.99 annually on renewal. A plan covering up to 25 devices was also listed at $134.99/£116.99 for the first year, with the same figure quoted for subsequent years.
A 30-day free trial is available after creating an account through Avira’s website, with no credit or debit card information required during the sign-up process.
Compared with using Avira Free Security for Mac, the appeal of Prime is therefore largely in the additional utilities and services. The core antivirus features remain strong, but Prime adds cleanup, application-removal, privacy, and VPN capabilities in one subscription.
Whether that’s good value depends on how many of these tools you’ll actually use. The Junk Cleaner and Uninstaller are useful additions, while the VPN is adequate for everyday purposes. The Identity Assistant’s failure to load, however, makes it difficult to recommend paying extra for its additional identity-monitoring coverage.
Avira Prime offers a lot of functionality, but the longer-term cost becomes harder to justify if you only need its antivirus capabilities.
How we tested
Avira Prime 2.3.10 was tested in-house on a MacBook Pro running macOS Tahoe 26.6.2.
Testing included more than 130 malware samples from the Objective-See Mac malware collection, with a focus on malware detection and removal, scanning behaviour, and the application’s ability to manage infected files and volumes.
Quick, Full, and Custom Scans were evaluated, including a Full Scan of more than 633GB of data. The suite’s additional features, including Phantom VPN, Password Manager, Cookie Cleaner, Identity Assistant, Junk Cleaner, Uninstaller, Startup Apps, and Scheduler, were also examined for functionality and ease of use.
Results were compared with independent AV-TEST laboratory findings where applicable.
Should you buy Avira Prime for Mac
The new version of Avira Prime proves to be one of the better antivirus and anti-malware utilities I’ve tested in some time, although there are still areas that need improvement.
Its malware scanning interface, scheduler, junk removal, and application-removal tools are genuinely impressive, and the overall suite offers a useful set of features without becoming excessively complicated.
The occasional malware components left behind during testing are a concern, while the Cookie Cleaner’s lack of search, limited scan-log exports, and the server-side error that made Identity Assistant impossible to evaluate all represent missed opportunities. The bare-bones VPN also won’t suit everyone, particularly users who need more advanced networking features. 
These issues aren’t necessarily deal-breakers, but they’re worth considering alongside the subscription price, especially after the introductory offer expires.
Despite these shortcomings, Avira Prime’s core security and maintenance functions remain strong. It’s well worth evaluating during the advertised 30-day trial to determine whether its combination of protection and additional utilities is right for you.
See how Avira Prime compares to other Mac antivirus solutions in our round up of the best.

title: Should you buy the MacBook Pro now or wait for the M6 or Touchscreen MacBook?
content:
Macworld





If you’re thinking of buying a MacBook Pro, it could be worth waiting a little longer. Apple is reportedly preparing two MacBook Pro updates for October 27, including a new entry-level model with the M6 chip and redesigned higher-end models featuring OLED touchscreens.
The standard 14-inch MacBook Pro is expected to gain Apple’s new M6 processor while retaining its existing design. The redesigned MacBook Pro models, meanwhile, could introduce thinner and lighter bodies, OLED touchscreens, and M5 Pro and M5 Max chips – becoming Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro.
With new models potentially arriving within weeks, we’d recommend waiting unless you need a MacBook Pro immediately or find a particularly good discount on the current M5 models. Apple increased MacBook Pro prices by $300 to $500 in June 2026, so discounts and refurbished models remain worth considering.
The MacBook Pro is best suited to creative professionals, software developers, engineers and other power users who need sustained performance, a premium display, plenty of ports and high memory configurations. If your workload consists mainly of web browsing, office work, studying or light creative tasks, the MacBook Air is likely to offer better value at a much lower price. In this guide, we’ll explain whether you should buy now or wait, which MacBook Pro is right for you, the best times of year to buy, today’s best deals, and whether a refurbished model or MacBook Air might be a better choice.


Should you buy a MacBook Pro now? 
With new MacBook Pro models reportedly arriving on October 27 2026, we’d recommend waiting before buying. The upcoming M6 model should bring better performance to the entry-level MacBook Pro, while the redesigned M5 Pro and M5 Max models could offer significant display and design improvements. However, the existing MacBook Pro lineup remains an excellent choice if you find a substantial discount.
Buy a MacBook Pro now if:
You’re upgrading from an Intel Mac: Apple is ending support for Intel Macs, so if you haven’t yet switched to Apple Silicon, now is a good time to do so. As Intel Macs reach the end of support, they’ll stop receiving security updates, leaving them vulnerable to newly discovered security flaws.
You need a new laptop: If your current Mac is broken, unreliable or slowing you down, there’s little reason to wait.
You edit video or create content: Whether you’re editing 4K video, working in Photoshop or Lightroom, producing music or creating 3D graphics, the MacBook Pro delivers the sustained performance creative professionals need.
You’re a software developer, engineer or AI professional: Compiling code, running virtual machines, working with AI models or processing large datasets is much faster on the MacBook Pro, particularly the M5 Pro and M5 Max models.
You need sustained performance: Unlike the fanless MacBook Air, the MacBook Pro uses active cooling to maintain peak performance during long exports, renders and other demanding workloads.
You need professional features: The MacBook Pro offers a Liquid Retina XDR display with ProMotion, HDMI, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe charging and higher memory and storage options than the MacBook Air.
You find an excellent deal: With new models expected on October 27, retailers may offer bigger discounts on the existing M5 lineup. If you don’t need the latest chip or touchscreen design, a discounted M5 MacBook Pro could be excellent value.


						

							


When shouldn’t you buy a MacBook Pro?
The MacBook Pro is an excellent laptop, but it isn’t the right choice for everyone. If you don’t need its extra performance or professional features, you’ll save money – and probably be just as happy – with a MacBook Air. There are also a few situations where it’s worth waiting rather than buying today.
Don’t buy a MacBook Pro now if:
You already own a recent MacBook Pro: If you have an M2, M3 or M4 MacBook Pro, the performance improvements offered by the M5 generation are relatively modest.
You’re waiting for the redesign: Apple is reportedly preparing OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models with thinner, lighter designs and M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for October 27.
You want the next-generation chips: The entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro is expected to gain the M6 chip on October 27, bringing improvements in CPU, GPU, and AI performance.
You’re looking for the best price: With new MacBook Pro models reportedly arriving soon, discounts on the existing M5 generation could become more attractive. Black Friday may bring further savings.
You mainly use your laptop for everyday tasks: If your workload consists of web browsing, Microsoft Office, streaming, email, video calls or light photo editing, a MacBook Air offers excellent performance for much less money.
You’re a student with basic computing needs: If your coursework mainly involves writing essays, researching online or creating presentations, a MacBook Air is likely to be the better value.
Portability is your priority: The MacBook Air is thinner, lighter and completely silent thanks to its fanless design.
You’re on a budget: The MacBook Air delivers outstanding performance for most users while costing significantly less than the MacBook Pro.
For most people, the MacBook Air is the better buy. The MacBook Pro only comes into its own if you regularly run demanding professional workloads that benefit from its active cooling, more powerful chips, superior display, additional ports and higher memory options.

When is the best time to buy a MacBook Pro?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




If you’re looking for the lowest price on a MacBook Pro, the best times to buy are during major sales events such as Amazon Prime Day in June/July or October and Black Friday.
Black Friday is typically the strongest shopping period for MacBook Pro deals, although the lowest prices are often reserved for older or clearance models, and popular configurations can sell out quickly.
Another time to look for deals is shortly after Apple launches a new model, as retailers often discount the previous generation to clear remaining stock, making it possible to save hundreds if you don’t need the latest chip.
If you’re a student, you can save all year. Students, teachers, and education staff can typically save $100 to $200 on a new MacBook Pro through Apple’s Education Store. However, the best time to buy is usually during Apple’s annual Back to School promotion in the summer, when qualifying customers can often claim a free pair of AirPods or another bonus gift alongside the education discount. Is buying a refurbished MacBook Pro a good idea?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Buying a refurbished MacBook Pro can be a great way to save money – particularly if you buy directly from Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store.
As of July 2026, buying refurbished makes more sense than ever because Apple has continued to sell refurbished Macs at pre-price-hike prices, allowing buyers to avoid the $300 to $500 increases Apple introduced on new MacBook Pro models in June.
Apple Certified Refurbished Macs are typically around 15% cheaper than brand-new models and come with the same one-year warranty, 90 days of complimentary technical support, and the option to purchase AppleCare+. Every Mac undergoes extensive testing, is cleaned and inspected, and receives genuine Apple replacement parts where necessary.
The main downside is availability. Stock changes daily, so you may need to wait for the exact model, storage capacity, memory configuration, or colour you want. Newer MacBook Pro models also usually don’t appear in the refurbished store until several months after launch.
Third-party retailers, including Amazon, also sell refurbished Macs, but quality standards vary considerably. We generally recommend avoiding Macs that are more than five years old, as they may receive fewer years of macOS and security updates. In some cases, retailers also offer larger discounts on new, previous-generation MacBook Pro models during major sales events, so it’s always worth comparing prices before you buy.
For most buyers, Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store remains the safest and best-value way to buy a refurbished MacBook Pro.

Which MacBook Pro to choose
Before choosing a MacBook Pro, bear in mind that Apple is reportedly preparing new models for October 27. The entry-level MacBook Pro is expected to gain the M6 processor, while the higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max models could receive an OLED touchscreen redesign. Unless you need a laptop immediately, we’d recommend waiting to compare the new models before buying.
Choose the M5 MacBook Pro if you want Pro features such as the better display, extra ports and active cooling, but don’t need the power of the M5 Pro or M5 Max.
Choose the M5 Pro MacBook Pro if you’re a professional who regularly edits 4K video, compiles large software projects, works with RAW photos, produces music or runs multiple demanding applications at once. For most creative professionals and developers, the M5 Pro offers the best balance of performance and price.
Choose the M5 Max MacBook Pro if your work pushes a laptop to its limits. The M5 Max is designed for users editing multiple streams of 8K video, creating complex 3D animations, running large AI or machine learning workloads, or handling visual effects and other GPU-intensive tasks. Unless you regularly perform these types of work, the M5 Pro is likely to offer better value. 


						

							


What about the MacBook Air?

				
					

				
			
The MacBook Air is a good alternative at a lower price.

Stephan Wiesend




If you’re considering a MacBook Pro, it’s also worth looking at the MacBook Air. Apple updated the Air in March 2026, and with a starting price of $1,299/£1,299 (the price increased by $200/£200 in June 2026), it’s significantly cheaper than the MacBook Pro.
The MacBook Air is a good choice if you:
Mainly browse the web, use Microsoft Office or stream media.
Are a student or home user with light computing needs.
Value portability and a silent, fanless design.
Want the best value MacBook.
However, the lower price comes with a few compromises. Compared to the MacBook Pro, the Air offers lower sustained performance, a less advanced display, fewer ports, and lower memory and storage limits.
Choose the MacBook Pro if you need:
Sustained performance for video editing, coding, 3D rendering or AI workloads.
A Liquid Retina XDR display with ProMotion and HDR.
More connectivity, including HDMI, an SDXC card slot and additional Thunderbolt ports.
Higher-end M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, with up to 128GB of unified memory.
For most everyday users, the MacBook Air is the better value. But if your work regularly pushes your laptop to its limits, the MacBook Pro is well worth the extra investment.


						

							


Do you need to upgrade your current Mac?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Whether you need to upgrade depends on three things: how old your Mac is, whether Apple still supports it, and whether it can keep up with the apps and features you use every day.
If you have an Intel Mac, it’s time to upgrade
With macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple has ended support for Intel Macs. While Apple is expected to continue providing security updates for the small number of Intel Macs that support macOS 26 Tahoe, that support is likely to last only another year or two.
The only Intel Macs that can run macOS Tahoe are:
16-inch MacBook Pro (2019)
13-inch MacBook Pro (2020, four Thunderbolt ports)
27-inch iMac (2020)
Mac Pro (2019)
If your Mac isn’t on this list, it may no longer receive the latest macOS updates and will eventually stop receiving security updates. For more advice, read How long Macs and MacBooks last: Lifespan, support and when to upgrade.
If you’re still using an Intel Mac, we recommend upgrading as soon as your budget allows. Moving from Intel to Apple Silicon is one of the biggest upgrades Apple has ever offered. You’ll benefit from dramatically faster performance, much longer battery life, quieter operation, Apple Intelligence support, and many more years of macOS compatibility. Read our guides to macOS Tahoe and macOS Golden Gate to see what you’ll gain by upgrading.


						

							


Which are the best retailers to buy a MacBook from?
Aside from Apple (View the MacBook Pro in the Apple Store and View the MacBook Pro in the Apple Store U.K). There are a number of third-party resellers that frequently discount the MacBook Pro.

The sci-fi adventure game is set in a procedurally-generated universe, filled with countless solar systems, planets, and space stations. Starting on the outer rim, players can explore unique planets, build bases, and upgrade their ships as they try to reach the center of the universe.

title: Apple Watch Ultra 1 vs. Ultra 4 Buyer's Guide: Is It Worth Upgrading?
content:
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 arrives four years after the original model. Across three subsequent generations, Apple added a brighter and larger display, satellite connectivity, new health sensors, more capable chips, and longer battery life. For owners of the original Ultra, are those cumulative improvements enough to justify upgrading now, or can their existing watch last another year?



Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at $799 in the U.S. Apple discontinued the original Ultra in 2023, and it no longer supports the latest major watchOS release. Here are the key differences between the two models:



Apple Watch Ultra (first-generation)
‌Apple Watch Ultra 4‌


Natural titanium finish
Natural and black titanium finishes

Wide-angle LTPO3 ‌OLED‌ display with 1Hz always-on updates, allowing supported faces to show ticking seconds


Up to 2,000 nits of brightness
Up to 3,000 nits of brightness; 1-nit minimum brightness


410 by 502 pixels; 1,185 sq mm display area
422 by 514 pixels; 1,245 sq mm display area (5% larger), with thinner display borders


Flashlight
Flashlight boost via Digital Crown

S11 chip


1GB RAM
4GB RAM

4-core Neural Engine



Secure Exclave for isolated audio processing


32GB storage
64GB storage



Single tap, Double Tap, and wrist flick gestures


Siri processed in the cloud via an internet connection
On-device ‌Siri‌ for supported requests, including access to and logging of health and fitness data

Improved on-device dictation



‌Siri‌ AI support

Second-generation Ultra Wideband chip

Precision Finding for compatible iPhone models, AirTag 2, and the AirPods Pro 3 charging case, with distance and direction guidance



Automatic Now Playing controls and Smart Stack media suggestions when near a HomePod


Electrical heart sensor and third-generation optical heart sensor
Health Sensing System with new electrical and always-on optical heart sensors


Background heart-rate measurements
Background heart-rate measurements every five seconds


Heart-rate variability (HRV) measurements
More frequent measurements of overall HRV and Recovery HRV


Overnight Vitals view
Overnight and daytime Vitals views



Readiness app



Sleep apnea notifications



Hypertension notifications


Blood Oxygen readings viewable on the watch
On affected U.S. models, Blood Oxygen readings are analyzed on the paired iPhone and viewed in its Health app


Step tracking and estimated indoor workout distance
More accurate all-day step tracking and indoor workout distance measurements, plus a Steps watch-face complication


Workout Buddy requires a nearby Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone
Enhanced Workout Buddy with additional insights and Spanish support



Live Translation in Messages when paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone


LTE and UMTS cellular connectivity
LTE and 5G cellular connectivity, with improved weak-signal reception through simultaneous use of both antennas



Emergency SOS, Messages, and Find My via satellite



Audio Intelligence: Sound Recognition, automatic music identification, Live Rewind, and ‌Siri‌ Recap


Built-in speakers for calls, alerts, and ‌Siri‌
Built-in speakers for calls, alerts, ‌Siri‌, and media playback

Charges from 0 to 80% in about 45 minutes; 15 minutes of charging for up to 18 hours of normal use; five minutes for up to 10 hours of sleep tracking

Natural titanium: 63.0 grams; black titanium: 63.1 grams

Dual-frequency GPS supporting GPS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou

Supports watchOS 27, including the ‌Siri‌ app, dynamic app grid, new Smart Stack suggestions, Call Context, and consolidated ‌Find My‌ app


Now discontinued
Starts at $799




Existing first-generation Apple Watch Ultra owners can reasonably keep their watch for another year if its battery still covers their usual days and workouts. Losing support for ‌watchOS 27‌ is significant, but it does not prevent the original Ultra from continuing to handle notifications, activity tracking, navigation, and its other existing features. Owners satisfied with those capabilities may prefer to eke out another year of use and wait to see whether next year's model offers a more substantial upgrade.

However, the Ultra 4 is a worthwhile upgrade for anyone already running into the original model's limitations. The new Health Sensing System provides more detailed heart-rate and recovery insights, while sleep apnea and hypertension notifications expand its health capabilities. These changes are most compelling if you will use the additional information to follow changes in your daily condition or adjust your training.

Longer battery life and satellite connectivity strengthen the case for owners who record extended workouts or regularly travel beyond cellular coverage. If your original Apple Watch Ultra now struggles to finish an outing without charging, the improved battery life is a practical reason to replace it. The larger, brighter display, newer gestures, Audio Intelligence, and expanded Precision Finding support also make the cumulative upgrade more noticeable in everyday use.

cannot run watchOS 27, so it misses ‌Siri‌ AI and the latest operating system's other additions. If those features would materially improve how you use your watch, waiting another year means accepting those limitations in the meantime.

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are premium true wireless earbuds from Apple. Released in September 2025, they add heart-rate monitoring, foam-infused eartips, stronger ANC, improved sound, longer battery life and IP57 water resistance.
Why we like them
The AirPods Pro 3 refine an already excellent formula with noticeably better comfort, stronger noise cancellation, richer sound and longer battery life while keeping the same launch price. Heart-rate tracking is a useful bonus, making them an easy recommendation for most Apple users.
Who are they best for
They’re ideal for iPhone users wanting premium wireless earbuds with excellent noise cancellation, secure all-day comfort and seamless Apple ecosystem integration. They’re especially appealing for fitness enthusiasts who can benefit from the new built-in heart-rate monitoring.

Verdict
The AirPods Pro 3 aren’t a revolutionary upgrade, but they successfully improve almost every aspect of Apple’s best earbuds. The Apple AirPods 5 (with Wireless Charging Case) are open-fit wireless earbuds featuring the H2 chip, improved Active Noise Cancellation, Adaptive Audio, Transparency mode, Conversation Awareness, and Personalized Spatial Audio. The $149/£139 version adds wireless charging, touch-sensitive volume controls, and a Find My speaker in the case.
Why we like them
The AirPods 5 bring better sound and stronger noise cancellation to Apple’s familiar open-ear design, while costing less than the AirPods 4 with ANC they replace. In the review from our sister website, Macwelt, the AirPods 5 were found to deliver a slightly richer, warmer sound than their predecessors and surprisingly effective noise cancellation, making them an excellent alternative to the more expensive AirPods Pro.
Who are they best for
They’re ideal for iPhone users who dislike silicone ear tips but still want effective ANC and premium features. They’re particularly well suited to everyday listening, commuting, and anyone who wants many of the AirPods Pro’s features without paying $249. The Wireless Charging Case version is the better choice for most buyers.
What are the biggest strengths
Rich, detailed sound with slightly warmer bass than AirPods 4
Excellent ANC for an open-ear design, particularly against steady background noise
Adaptive Audio and improved Transparency mode
Convenient swipe controls for adjusting volume
Wireless charging via Qi or an Apple Watch charger
Find My speaker built into the charging case
What are the compromises
Open design limits noise isolation compared with AirPods Pro
Fit remains unchanged from AirPods 4 and depends on ear shape
Higher-frequency sounds, including keyboard clicks, remain noticeable
Battery life trails many competing earbuds
No heart-rate monitoring or AirPods Pro hearing-health features
Discounted AirPods Pro 3 can narrow the price gap
What is battery life like
Apple rates the Wireless Charging Case model for up to five hours with ANC enabled, or seven hours with noise control off. The case extends ANC listening time to 22 hours. Macwelt’s testing achieved approximately four hours and 45 minutes indoors, dropping to four hours and 15 minutes when traveling with higher volume settings and Spatial Audio enabled.
How good is the ANC
Noise cancellation is particularly impressive for earbuds that don’t seal the ear canal. Macwelt’s testing found that the AirPods 5 effectively reduced steady background sounds, including road noise and computer fans. Apple claims up to 50 percent better noise cancellation than AirPods 4 with ANC. However, sharper sounds still get through, and the AirPods Pro 3 provide significantly stronger isolation.
What about the cheaper AirPods 5?
Apple also sells the standard AirPods 5 for $129/£119. These include the same H2 chip, sound improvements, and ANC, but have a USB-C-only charging case without wireless charging or a Find My speaker. They also lack the stem-based volume controls and have slightly shorter battery life, offering four hours with ANC and 20 hours with the case. For just $20/£20 more, the Wireless Charging Case model is worth the upgrade, although the cheaper version remains excellent value.
Verdict
The AirPods 5 (with Wireless Charging Case) are among the best open-ear wireless earbuds available. They combine richer sound, impressively effective noise cancellation, useful smart features, and convenient wireless charging at a lower price than their predecessors. Battery life is still fairly modest, and the unchanged fit won’t suit everyone, but they’re an excellent everyday choice for iPhone users who prefer an open design. With the added convenience of volume controls and wireless charging for just $20 more than the standard model, they’re the AirPods 5 we’d recommend.

Although the newer AirPods 5 now include ANC at a lower starting price, the Beats offer a more traditional in-ear design with silicone tips for a better seal, intuitive physical controls and stronger Android compatibility. They can also be excellent value when discounted.
Who are they best for
They are best for iPhone, iPad and Mac users wanting premium everyday earbuds with strong ANC, comfortable all-day wear and effortless Apple ecosystem integration. Frequent travellers, commuters and users interested in hearing health features will benefit most. 
What are the biggest strengths
Richer, clearer sound with significantly stronger bass
Excellent Active Noise Cancellation for travel and commuting
Best-in-class Transparency mode with Adaptive Transparency
Comfortable fit with four ear tip sizes, including XS
Handy swipe volume controls on each earbud
Deep Apple ecosystem integration with useful smart features 
What are the compromises
More expensive than many rivals
Better pure sound quality available elsewhere
No lossless, hi-res or LE Audio support

Most advanced features require Apple devices
Six-hour battery trails some competitors 
What is battery life like
Battery life is rated at up to six hours of listening from the earbuds on a charge, with around 24 hours total using the charging case. Apple Watch charging is also supported. 
How good is the ANC
Active Noise Cancellation is excellent, blocking substantially more outside noise than the original AirPods Pro. Adaptive Transparency intelligently reduces sudden loud sounds while still allowing important environmental sounds to remain audible. 
Verdict 
The AirPods Pro 2 remain among the best premium wireless earbuds for Apple users. They combine impressive sound quality, highly effective ANC, exceptional transparency mode and excellent ecosystem integration in a comfortable, refined package. While audiophiles can find better-sounding alternatives and battery life isn’t class-leading, the overall user experience is polished, reliable and difficult to beat within Apple’s ecosystem. As long as you can find them on sale.

How good is the ANC?

Verdict

Their engaging audio, comfortable design and long battery life make them highly appealing, even if the ANC, wireless charging and feature set don’t quite match the very best competitors. For music-first buyers, they’re easy to recommend.

							
		
We’re comparing all the best earbuds with Apple’s own offerings: the AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4 and AirPods 4 with ANC. Also included are various options from Apple-owned subsidiary Beats, which by association benefits from a lot of Apple-specific features. But just how well do they compete with headphones from the likes of Bose, Sennheiser, Bowers & Wilkins and Sony? 
How to choose earbud headphones
There are a few factors to consider before you hit that buy button.
Type
Earbuds, or in-ear headphones, typically fall into three main categories:
Earbuds – the type of headphones included with every iPhone and iPod and sit loosely in your outer ears. Although earbuds don’t produce outstanding sound, they’re compact and relatively inexpensive. Apple’s stock ‘buds are actually decent as earbuds go; you’re not going to get a huge upgrade in sound quality by simply replacing them with a different model. Still, there are a few alternatives out there that provide modest improvements if you’re looking for a new set. Recommendations:
In-Ear-Canal Headphones: These headphones, also known as canalphones, use silicone or foam eartips that fit snugly—and fairly deep—in your ear canals. Like earplugs, they block most external noise, so they’re great for travel and noisy environments. They’re also capable of producing stunning audio quality. On the other hand, some people find canalphones to be uncomfortable, and the best ones come with an equally stunning price tag. If you decide to spend the big bucks on a set of high-end canalphones, we enthusiastically recommend going all-in and getting custom eartips—tips custom-made for your particular ears. The process requires an audiologist visit to get impressions taken of your ears, but the benefits include substantially better comfort. (On some models, you may gain better noise isolation and better sound quality, as well.) A step above custom eartips are custom in-ear monitors, which place the actual headphone circuitry in larger, custom-made earpieces.
Canalbuds: Canalbuds, which occupy a middle ground between earbuds and in-ear-canal models, have become quite popular. Compared to canalphones, canalbuds generally use smaller eartips that sit just inside the ends of your ear canals instead of deep inside them. Good canalbuds easily best earbuds in terms of audio performance and noise isolation, but fall short of good canalphones in those areas. On the other hand, canalbuds tend to be more comfortable than true canalphones because they don’t sit so deep and don’t fit so tightly; they’re also usually less expensive. (See our in-ear-canal-headphone primer, linked above, for more information on canalbuds.)
Battery life
This is crucial as many in-ear headphones have tiny batteries that help to keep the weight down but may only last for a few hours. That might be fine if you just want to listen to some music while you’re working out, but won’t be much use on a long journey by train or plane.
However, some in-ear headphones, such as Apple’s AirPods, also include a charging case that can top up the battery, so that’s something you should check on before buying any in-ear headphones.
Noise canceling
Some headphones are specifically designed for people who travel a lot or use headphones in noisy conditions and provide active noise-canceling (ANC) option that helps to block out background noise on trains and planes – although this can add quite a lot to the overall price of the headphones.
Note this isn’t to be confused with passive noise isolation (or often referred to as canceling), which is just the way physically having headphones in/on blocks sound – like putting earplugs or ear defenders on.
Sound quality
We’d always recommend trying out any new headphones in a store or showroom whenever possible, but we realise that’s not always practical or hygenic.
Compatibility
Most wireless headphones support Apple’s preferred AAC Bluetooth codec, ensuring good compatibility with iPhones, iPads and Macs. Many also support additional codecs such as aptX Adaptive, aptX Lossless, LDAC or LC3/LE Audio, which can deliver higher bit rates, lower latency or improved efficiency when paired with compatible Android phones and other devices.
Apple devices have never supported Qualcomm’s aptX family of codecs, instead relying on AAC for Bluetooth audio. While this has often been attributed to Apple’s preference for controlling its own audio ecosystem, it also means Apple users can’t take advantage of newer Qualcomm codecs such as aptX Adaptive or aptX Lossless when using third-party headphones.
That isn’t necessarily the drawback it once was. AAC remains a very capable codec, and Apple’s implementation is widely regarded as one of the best, delivering consistent sound quality and excellent battery efficiency. However, Android users with compatible devices may be able to enjoy higher-resolution or lower-latency wireless audio through codecs such as LDAC or aptX Lossless.
For Apple users, the most important thing is that headphones support AAC, as this provides the best wireless experience across iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch. If a pair also supports codecs such as aptX Adaptive or LDAC, that’s a useful bonus if you also own Android devices or other compatible hardware.
There are a few exceptions. Some premium headphones and earbuds, such as the Bowers & Wilkins Pi8, include a smart charging case that can act as a wireless audio transmitter. By connecting the case directly to a USB-C or 3.5mm audio source, it can stream audio to the earbuds using aptX Adaptive, bypassing the Bluetooth limitations of the source device and potentially improving sound quality and reducing latency.
It’s also worth noting that all of the Bluetooth headphones featured here work with Apple Watch, making them ideal for workouts, runs and listening on the go.

title: Last-minute leak reveals key details about Apple’s ‘HomeView’ hub
content:
Macworld





Tomorrow’s Welcome Home Apple event–sorry, “experience”–will center on the smart home. And at the core of that home sits Apple’s new home hub, from which all the other devices will be monitored and controlled. Thanks to a last-minute report we now know, or at any rate have been told, a great deal about what Apple has in store for this vital product.
In the latest instalment of his Power On newsletter, Bloomberg leaker Mark Gurman claims to reveal a wide range of key details about Apple’s imminent smart home hub, including its name, launch timeframe, design, usage, and software. He also discusses the other products that Apple will announce alongside it, including the new Apple TV and HomePod mini.
Firstly, the hub won’t be called HomePad or HomeHub, as some pundits had expected, but “HomeView.” Gurman credits this scoop to MacRumors, which on Friday spotted suspicious trademark activity by a shell company.
He says this branding “reflects how the device is meant to be used.” It’s a product you mainly look at (and speak to using Siri AI) rather than interacting with it directly via touch, even though the latter input method is possible using the small touchscreen. He believes that a name like HomePad would have led customers to expect more of a touch-centered experience, similar to the iPad.
On the software front, don’t expect an App Store for third-party software, or indeed a wide range of first-party applications. Rather, the HomeView will “support a limited selection of Apple applications.” Perhaps this will change in the future, bearing in mind that the original iPhone didn’t have an App Store either, but in this case it appears to be more of an intentional decision to focus on simplicity of use.
Design-wise, the HomeView (as we’ve known for some time) will come in two versions. A countertop version with a metal speaker base will come in many of Apple’s classic colors: Space Gray, silver, Starlight, and pink. But the wall-mounted version will only come in Space Gray and silver. In both cases, the device will run an A18 processor and serve “as the Siri command center for an Apple-powered household.”
For the first month or so of this new era for the smart home, however, Apple-powered households will be without their command center. The hardware will land in stores at different times: the new HomePod mini and Apple TV on October 30; the HomeView in mid-November; and the LG accessories “later this year at the earliest.” This seems a little uncoordinated, but Apple has shown an appetite in recent years for announcing things before they’re ready. Indeed, the iPhone Duo, unveiled as long ago as September 9, won’t go on sale until October 23.
The announcements are scheduled for October 13 at 9 am ET. You can follow the latest breaking news as it happens with our Welcome Home live blog, which is already up and running.

title: Every new Apple product coming in 2026 & 2027
content:
Macworld





It’s been a huge year for Apple, with a wave of new products arriving throughout 2026. The year began with the MacBook Neo and iPhone 17e in March, followed by the new Mac mini and Mac Studio in August.
September brought another major wave of launches at Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, including the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5.
But Apple isn’t finished yet. The company has confirmed a “Welcome Home” gathering for October 13, where new smart-home products are expected to debut. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman also reports that further Mac and iPad announcements are planned for October 27, although Apple has yet to confirm that date.
Apple has also rolled out its major operating-system updates for 2026, including iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27, alongside updates for the Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Vision Pro.
With most of Apple’s biggest launches already behind us, attention is turning to what’s next. New iPads, smart-home devices, and potentially Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro could still arrive before the end of the year, while smart glasses and other products may follow in 2027. Here’s everything Apple has launched in 2026 so far – and what’s still to come.
Apple’s roadmap: At a glance
As of September 1, 2026, Apple’s roadmap has come under the direction of CEO John Ternus. Former CEO Tim Cook has moved into the executive chairman role. The shift from an operations-focused leader to one with deep hardware engineering roots could signal a more product-driven approach – and a renewed emphasis on standout hardware.

Every New Apple Product Launched in 2026… so far
Here is what Apple has already announced in 2026:

Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4: Faster chips, Apple’s latest health-sensing features: Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4.
AirPods 5: Stronger open-ear Active Noise Cancellation and longer battery life: AirPods 5.
Mac mini M6 and M5 Pro: Faster storage, upgraded connectivity, and a strong focus on AI performance: New Mac mini 2026 guide.
Mac Studio M5 Max and M5 Ultra: Faster AI and graphics performance, increased memory bandwidth: New Mac Studio 2026 guide.
AirPods Max 2: Improved audio and the H2 chip. Find out more here: AirPods Max 2 guide.
MacBook Neo: Apple’s brand new, low-cost Mac laptop. Find out more here: MacBook Neo guide.
MacBook Air M5: Now with the M5 chip. Read about the 2026 MacBook Air here: MacBook Air M5 guide.
MacBook Pro M5 Pro & M5 Max: A significant upgrade over the M4 series. Read: MacBook Pro M5 Pro & Max guide.
Studio Display: Finally gets Thunderbolt 5 and a better webcam. 
Studio Display XDR: With mini-LED technology and ProMotion up to 120Hz.
iPhone 17e: The new, entry-level, iPhone replaces the iPhone 16e. Read more here: iPhone 17e guide.
iPad Air M4: The iPad Air now has an M4 chip. Read more here: iPad Air M4 guide.
AirTag 2: Four years on Apple updated the AirTag, read our review here: AirTag 2nd gen review.
And… RIP Mac Pro: Apple has confirmed that it is discontinuing its tower workstation.  
Read on to find out what new products to expect at Apple’s next event and throughout 2026.


						

							







Every New Apple Product Launching in 2026
In the sections below we’ve split the upcoming new products into categories including Mac, iPad, iPhone, Apple Watch, Home, AirPods, and some new product categories.
Apple Intelligence and Siri updates still coming in 2026
Apple released iOS 27, iPadOS 27 and its other major software updates in September, bringing the new Siri AI experience, expanded Apple Intelligence features, parental controls and a range of improvements across Apple’s apps and operating systems.
But Apple’s 2026 software rollout isn’t finished. Siri AI is still being rolled out to eligible users, with access depending on device, language and region, and Apple has already begun testing the updates that will follow the initial iOS 27 and macOS 27 releases.
Siri and Apple Intelligence
Siri AI arrived with iOS 27 as a substantially redesigned version of Apple’s voice assistant, with improved conversational abilities, personal-context awareness, onscreen awareness and the ability to carry out more actions across apps. However, not every Apple device can run the new features, and some users may still need to join a waiting list before gaining access.
Apple is also expanding Siri AI beyond its initial English-language launch. Additional language support is due during the remainder of 2026, while regional restrictions mean some Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features remain unavailable in parts of the world. 
Upcoming iOS 27 and macOS updates
iOS 27 itself is already available, but Apple is continuing development through iOS 27.x updates. These releases are expected to deliver additional features, refinements and bug fixes throughout the remainder of 2026, with Apple’s beta program providing an early indication of what is coming next.
The same applies to iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27 and Apple’s other platforms, which will continue to receive point updates following their initial September releases. Find out about the latest iOS beta and latest macOS beta.  


						

							


What new iPads are coming in 2026/2027 

				
					

				
			
Screenshot

Foundry




Don’t expect major redesigns for the iPads this year. Instead, Apple is likely to focus on faster chips and other internal upgrades. That said, both the iPad and iPad mini are due for an update – particularly the entry-level iPad, which currently lacks support for Apple Intelligence. Here’s what we expect Apple to announce:
iPad mini
Expected announcement: October 27, according to Bloomberg; unconfirmed.
The next iPad mini could be one of Apple’s biggest remaining upgrades of the year. Multiple reports point to Apple replacing the current 8.3-inch LCD with an OLED display, potentially increasing the screen size slightly to around 8.5 inches while keeping the overall dimensions much the same. Samsung Display is also reported to have begun mass-producing OLED panels for the new model, suggesting the launch is getting closer.
The latest reporting points to the A20 Pro chip – as used in the iPhone 18 Pro. Earlier references suggested the A19 Pro, but more recent findings in Apple code favor the newer processor. 
Other upgrades could include Apple’s N1 networking chip, bringing Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread, while cellular models are expected to adopt Apple’s C1X modem. Apple may also move the front camera to the landscape edge, bringing the iPad mini into line with the rest of the current iPad range.
Apple is also reportedly working on a more water-resistant design. Bloomberg has reported that this could involve a new vibration-based speaker system that would allow Apple to eliminate conventional speaker holes and improve sealing. Bloomberg points to an October 27 announcement, although Apple has not confirmed the date. Read our round up of iPad mini rumors.
iPad 
Late 2026 update possible
When the standard iPad was updated in March 11, 2025, the biggest disappointment was that it featured a A16 chip and therefore didn’t support Apple Intelligence. Apple looks set to rectify that in 2026 with an upgrade to the A18 or A19 chip, with the latter offering 50% better performance. The release timeline for an iPad with an A18 or A19 chip is anticipated before the end of 2026, in fact, Apple code suggests the company may be planning an update sooner-rather-than-later.
Read more about the 2026 iPad in our rumor round up. 
Should you buy now or wait? 
With the iPad prices increasing in June 2026, you may want to hold off buying one now. If you are going to pay more at least get the most up-to-date model, or buy from Apple’s Refurbished Store to get a bargain. Read Should I buy an iPad now or wait?


						

							


Which new Macs are coming in 2026/2027?
2026 is expected to be a significant year for the Mac, with Apple’s first touchscreen Mac rumored as part of a MacBook Pro redesign. March 3 saw the launch of the M5 MacBook Air and M5 Pro/M5 Max MacBook Pro and March 4 saw Apple introduce a new entry-level laptop – the $599 MacBook Neo.
The long expected Mac Studio and Mac mini updates came in August 2026 and went on sale September 22, although some high-memory Mac Studio configurations won’t arrive until later. These Macs have become popular for running AI models locally; however, global RAM shortages – driven by AI companies purchasing large amounts of memory for data centres – have been having a knock-on effect on availability during 2026 and these RAM shortages have also had an effect on prices, with Mac prices increasing by $300 to $500 in June and in the case of the Mac mini, by a further $100 with the 2026 launch.
One Mac that won’t be getting an update is the long-neglected Mac Pro. Apple has confirmed that the Mac Pro will be discontinued in favor of the Mac Studio.
Touchscreen MacBook Pro
Expected announcement: October 27, according to Bloomberg; unconfirmed.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro is expected to feature an OLED touchscreen and a substantially lighter body. However, Mark Gurman has played down earlier suggestions that it will be significantly thinner. Reports point to the use of M5 Pro and M5 Max processors to enable Apple to keep the project on schedule.
Read the rumors about the MacBook Pro with a touch screen.
M6 MacBook Pro 
Expected announcement: October 27, according to Bloomberg; unconfirmed.
Apple is expected to update the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip. This would be a separate update from the rumored OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro, which is expected to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
Gurman includes this model among the products reportedly planned for October 27. 
Read more about the rumored M6 MacBook Pro.
iMac
Expected announcement: October 27, according to Bloomberg; unconfirmed.
Apple is reportedly preparing an M6 iMac, skipping the M5 generation following the M4 model introduced in October 2024. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman expects the update before the end of 2026, with new color options but no major redesign.
Gurman’s October 8 report specifically named the M6 iMac among the products planned for October 27. 
Read more about the rumored M6 iMac and new colors. Also read about the larger iMac rumors.
Should you buy now or wait? 
With the prices of Macs increasing in June due to the global RAM shortages you may want to hold off buying one now. If you are going to pay more at least get the most up-to-date model, or buy from Apple’s Refurbished Store to get a bargain. Read the following for more guidance:
Should you buy the MacBook Pro now or wait? 
Should you buy the MacBook Air now or wait?
Should you buy a Mac mini now or wait?
Should you buy a Mac Studio now or wait?


						

							


AirPod updates coming in 2027
According to a brief update in Mark Gurman’s Power On newsletter for Bloomberg in August, Apple is aiming to launch camera-equipped AirPods.
The new earbuds are expected to resemble the AirPods Pro 3, although it’s not yet clear whether they will also include a heart rate sensor.
The cameras are said to include both visible-light and infrared sensors, but they reportedly won’t be designed for taking photos or recording video, as their placement and image quality would make them unsuitable for those tasks. Instead, the cameras are expected to enable AI-powered features, such as hand gesture recognition, adapting audio based on the surrounding environment, and detecting whether someone is speaking directly to you or simply talking nearby.


						

							


Apple smart home products coming in 2026
Apple appears to be preparing a major expansion of its smart-home lineup , with several new devices reportedly close to launch. The products are expected to make much greater use of Siri AI, which current HomePod and Apple TV hardware lacks the processing power to support fully.
HomePod mini 2
Expected announcement: October 13; product availability unconfirmed.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The HomePod mini is finally expected to get its first major hardware update since the original model launched in 2020. The biggest change is likely to be a more powerful processor capable of supporting Apple’s new Siri AI features.
Recent references found in Apple code also point to updated colors, with black, blue, green, pink and white apparently replacing the current selection. Previous reports have also suggested upgraded wireless hardware, potentially including Apple’s own networking chip and newer Ultra Wideband technology.
The new HomePod mini is expected to be announced at Apple’s October 13 gathering.
HomePad smart home hub
Expected announcement: October 13; product availability unconfirmed.
Apple is reportedly preparing an entirely new smart-home device, often referred to as the HomePad. It is expected to feature a roughly 6-inch diagonal square display (which we estimate would measure around 4.25 inches square) and act as a central controller for HomeKit accessories, while also supporting FaceTime calls, music, widgets and Siri AI. It is expected to remain plugged in rather than function as a portable tablet.
Reports suggest Apple has developed both wall-mounted and speaker-base versions. The interface could combine elements of watchOS and tvOS, with glanceable widgets and controls designed specifically for use around the home.
Apple has confirmed a “Welcome Home” media gathering in New York on October 13. The rumored HomePad is expected to appear, although Apple has not confirmed this..
Updated HomePod mini and Apple TV 4K models could join the HomePad, but it is unclear whether all three would launch together. 
Read more: New HomePod rumors
Apple TV
Expected: Late 2026
A new Apple TV is expected with a faster processor capable of supporting Siri AI and upgraded wireless connectivity. Apple’s tvOS code has already included Apple Intelligence frameworks for future Apple TV and HomePod hardware, suggesting the next models will have significantly more capable chips than the current generation. More recently, an Apple support document has surfaced that references a 3rd generation or later Apple TV, the “or later” is leading people to suspect that the 4th generation Apple TV 4K could launch soon. 
HomePod with a display
Expected: 2027 or later
Apple has also been linked with a more advanced HomePod featuring a built-in display. This is sometimes referred to in reports as the HomePod Touch, although that is not an official Apple name.
Unlike the HomePad, which would primarily function as a standalone smart-home hub, this device is expected to combine a traditional HomePod speaker with a touchscreen display. Reports have also described more ambitious versions with a display mounted on a robotic arm, although those appear to be further away.
Because several different prototypes and form factors have been reported, it is possible that some of these rumors refer to different generations of the same broader product rather than several separate devices.


						

							


What new iPhones are coming in 2027?

				
					

				
			There are new iPhones coming.
Foundry




Based on current industry analysis and supply chain information, Apple has some significant changes planned for the iPhone in 2027, with an 20th anniversary iPhone rumored as well as the iPhone 18, 18e and iPhone Air 2.
iPhone 18 & iPhone 18e
Spring 2027 launch expected
Reports suggest that Apple could delay the iPhone 18 and release that handset alongside the iPhone 18e in the spring of 2027.
iPhone Air 2
The iPhone Air could also be getting an update. But there are rumors that it will actually merge with the iPhone 18. See our iPhone Air 2 rumors.

With the iPhone 18 launch not expected until the spring, now is a good time to buy an iPhone 17. Read: When is the best time to buy an iPhone.
However, prices have already risen across the board, so it is no longer possible to beat the price hikes unless you find a refurbished iPhone.


						

							


Upcoming Vision devices, AR and spatial computing
Apple Smart Glasses 
Possible 2026 introduction, 2027 launch
Unlike the bulky Vision Pro headset, the upcoming smart glasses from Apple are expected to follow a form factor similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses. This will be Apple’s first product built specifically for “Visual Intelligence.” It will likely handle tasks such as live translations, music playback, phone calls, and turn-by-turn directions. Prior to 2026, Apple’s spatial computing strategy has focused on the high-end market, but reports indicate a more affordable version of the headset is in development. Apple has reportedly paused work on a successor to the high-end Vision Pro and will instead release a cheaper Vision Pro.

title: We’re about to find out if Apple is serious about the smart home
content:
Macworld





A little over a decade ago, on September 13, 2016, Apple officially entered the smart-home market. That was the date when the Home app launched, bringing control of compatible third-party smart-home products to the iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Apple TV.
It’s probably fair to say that Home hasn’t exactly set the world on fire. Not like the AirPods, for instance, which launched a week earlier and went on to become one of Apple’s most popular and instantly recognisable products. Or like the Apple Watch, which came out the year before and quickly dominated the smartwatch market to such an effortless extent that it sometimes feels like the other watches might as well not bother.
I don’t choose those examples at random. Over the past couple of weeks, I’ve been reviewing the latest Apple Watch and the latest set of AirPods, which is why they’re in my thoughts. They’re both good products, but it’s particularly striking how much of the winning formula was there from the very beginning. Neither of those products change very much from year to year because they don’t need to. Apple got it right the first time, and now just needs to tweak and iterate.
The Home app was never quite like that, which I suspect is one of the reasons why it has never reached the same level of success. It didn’t come charging out of the gate the way the AirPods did, all confident design and omnipresent ads. It didn’t have the same marketing push behind it, the same level of visibility on Apple’s website. Home didn’t feel like a proper first-party product, just a vague umbrella concept for third-party accessories with varying levels of polish. The problem is that, uncharacteristically, Apple didn’t commit.
This week is Apple’s chance to renew its vows to the smart-home market and commit properly. Tomorrow, October 13, Apple holds its latest “Special Experience,” and the theme is hardly a secret: The tagline is “Welcome Home” and rumors of imminent launches have been unavoidable for weeks.
Apple is about to give the smart home another try. It will do this, most pundits agree, with an updated HomePod mini and Apple TV, along with something completely new: a home hub that looks a bit like half an iPad sitting on half a HomePod. Nobody is sure what this latter product will be called. HomePad is both obvious and logical, but it’s also rather boring. HomeHub is another option. My money is on something suitably new, such as the latest rumors suggest, HomeView.
Exciting new Apple hardware is a good start, and the HomeHub (let’s stick with that for now) would represent a gratifying statement of intent in being so obviously targeted at the smart home in a way no other first-party Apple product has been. The iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, and later HomePod could all be used to control home tech, but they had other purposes too. Without the home element, the HomeHub would seem rather pointless. It’s a risk. It’s a commitment.
But a smart-home ecosystem lives and dies by its lights, thermostats, doorbells, locks, and security cameras, not by the hub units which control them. And in that sphere Apple is still reluctant to commit.
Rumor says the company is about to unveil a suite of such products—all major categories except lights have been mentioned—but that they have been developed in partnership with LG and will be branded under that company’s name. (It was later claimed that Schneider is also involved, which may be a hint that further companies may feature at the event.) Some have described this as a second-party arrangement, which is an improvement of sorts. But it’s hard to imagine that LG accessories will trigger the same feelings of trust and goodwill as a set of Apple-branded home products.
Apple, of course, is not a company with experience in making doorbells and thermostats, and it’s understandable that it would be reluctant to start now. Working strategically with other companies, drawing on their expertise in niche markets, is a good thing. But this week Apple fans need to see that the company is prepared to commit fully to the smart home. And if it isn’t, we can hardly be expected to do the same.
